page.whatIsTitle: What is a Hash Generator?
page.whatIs:
A hash generator calculates a digest, a fixed string of hexadecimal characters that stands in for a particular input. The same bytes always produce the same digest and a single changed character changes much of the result. That behaviour is useful when you want to compare a downloaded file with its publisher's checksum or record a fingerprint without keeping the original. This tool exposes three SHA algorithms through the Web Crypto API and computes every digest in the current browser tab.

The algorithm switch controls the length. SHA-1 returns 160 bits, written as 40 hex characters, and is kept only for legacy checksums because collisions have been demonstrated. SHA-256 returns 256 bits, or 64 hex characters, and is the usual choice for integrity checks. SHA-512 returns 512 bits, or 128 hex characters, for systems that expect a longer value. The digest block below the input shows lowercase hex, while the two stat cards report the same length in bits and bytes.

Text is encoded as UTF-8 before hashing, so emoji and accented letters contribute their real byte sequences. A trailing space or a Windows line ending produces a different digest than the same visible words on another platform. Files are read as raw bytes and never decoded, which means one flipped bit anywhere changes the result. Web Crypto is available only in a secure context, so the page must be served over HTTPS or from localhost. Calculation happens after a short pause while you type and stale requests are discarded, so the digest always matches the text currently in the box.
page.exampleInput: hello
page.exampleNote: Verified SHA-256 digest of the UTF-8 bytes of hello. Leave the switch on SHA-256, type the same word with no trailing space, and the digest block will match the value shown here.
page.features:
SHA-1::160 bits, written as 40 hex characters. Available in the algorithm switch for legacy checks only, since collisions make it unsafe for new security decisions.
SHA-256::256 bits, written as 64 hex characters. The default choice in the switch for text and file integrity checks.
SHA-512::512 bits, written as 128 hex characters. Pick it in the switch when a downstream system expects a longer digest.
Web Crypto::The browser's subtle.digest method computes the value locally. Nothing is sent to a server and there is no salt or key.
Secure context::Web Crypto works only on HTTPS or localhost. Over plain HTTP the tool shows an actionable error instead of hashing.
page.mistakes:
Picking SHA-1 for a new check::It has 160 bits and known collisions. Use SHA-256 unless a legacy system requires the shorter digest.
Hashing text with hidden whitespace::A trailing space or pasted line break changes the UTF-8 bytes, so the digest will not match a clean copy.
Expecting to reverse a digest::A hash is not encryption. You cannot recover the original text or file from the hex string.
Comparing different algorithms::SHA-256 and SHA-512 produce different lengths for the same input, so choose the same algorithm on both sides.
page.limits:
Text is capped at 100,000 characters and files at 20 MB.
Web Crypto requires HTTPS or localhost; plain HTTP cannot produce a digest.
Very large files may take a moment on slower devices.
The tool creates plain digests, not salted password hashes or HMACs.
page.faqs:
Is my text or file uploaded anywhere?::No. The digest is calculated by the Web Crypto API inside this browser tab. Text is encoded locally and files are read as bytes, then discarded when you clear the input or close the page. Nothing is logged or sent to a server, so the hash reflects only what you can see.
Why is SHA-1 flagged with a warning?::SHA-1 produces a 160-bit digest, but researchers have shown practical collisions where two different inputs share one value. That makes it unsuitable for signatures or new security checks. It stays in the switch so you can reproduce legacy checksums, with a warning beside the control.
What is the SHA-256 digest of hello?::It is 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824. The example on this page uses that exact value. Type hello with no trailing space, leave the switch on SHA-256, and the digest block will match it. Changing the case gives a different result.
Can I hash a file larger than 20 MB?::Not in this tool. Files above 20 MB are rejected before reading because the browser must hold the bytes in memory to digest them. Use a local hashing command for very large archives, or split the data into smaller parts that each fit under the limit.
Why does the same word give a different digest elsewhere?::Check the algorithm first, because SHA-256 and SHA-512 return different lengths. Then look for invisible characters: a trailing space, a pasted line break or a different text encoding changes the bytes that Web Crypto hashes. Compare the exact same characters to get the same digest.
Does this work over plain HTTP?::No. Web Crypto's digest method needs a secure context, which means HTTPS or localhost. On an ordinary HTTP page the tool shows an actionable error explaining how to fix it. Current Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge support all three SHA options once the page is secure.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. The Web Crypto subtle.digest call uses the exact algorithm names SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512, so results match other standards-compliant tools. Reviewed 25 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an Image Resizer?
page.whatIs:
An image resizer changes the pixel grid of a picture, replacing the original width and height with new numbers. Shrinking a photo removes pixel data and usually reduces file size. Enlarging it adds interpolated pixels that cannot restore detail the camera never captured. This tool decodes your image locally, so the file is not uploaded anywhere.

Width, height and the aspect lock sit in the input pane. Width lock treats the width field as authoritative and derives the height from the source ratio. Height lock does the reverse. Unlocked mode fits your two numbers inside a bounding box without stretching the picture, so a 1600 by 1200 photo asked for 800 by 800 becomes 800 by 600. Output sides are rounded to whole pixels.

The format selector and quality slider sit in the result pane beside Download because they control encoding rather than geometry. JPEG is lossy and has no alpha channel, so transparent areas are flattened onto the page surface. PNG is lossless and keeps alpha, which often makes the file larger; quality has no effect and the slider is disabled. WebP can be lossy or lossless and is a good choice when you want small files with transparency.

After each change the canvas re-encodes the image and the result pane shows a preview, exact output dimensions, byte size and the percentage saved against the original. Files are limited to 20 MB and each output side to 8192 pixels, since larger canvases fail on many browsers. The sample button creates a simple image locally if you want to try the flow without a test file.
page.howToTitle: How to use Image Resizer
page.howTo:
Drop a JPEG, PNG or WebP image onto the drop zone or use the file picker.
Enter a width and height in pixels, then choose width lock, height lock or unlocked.
Pick an output format and, for JPEG or WebP, drag the quality slider beside Download.
Read the preview, output pixels, file size and saved percentage in the result pane.
Download the resized image with the correct extension.
page.features:
JPEG::Lossy format from the selector. Small files for photos, but no alpha channel: transparent pixels are flattened before encoding.
PNG::Lossless format from the selector. Keeps transparency and fine lines, so files are often bigger and the quality slider is disabled.
WebP::Modern format from the selector. Supports lossy compression with good detail at small sizes and also handles lossless encoding with alpha.
Quality::The slider beside Download affects lossy JPEG and WebP only. Lower values reduce bytes at the cost of detail; PNG output is unchanged.
page.mistakes:
Stretching to fill both fields::Unlocked mode fits inside the bounds instead of filling them. Choose a lock when one side must be exact.
Asking for detail back::Upscaling interpolates pixels. It cannot restore texture that was not in the source image.
Exporting transparency as JPEG::JPEG has no alpha channel, so the tool flattens transparent areas. Choose PNG or WebP if you need them.
Ignoring quality for PNG::PNG is lossless, so the slider is disabled. Switching format is the only way to trade fidelity for size.
page.limits:
Files above 20 MB are rejected before decoding.
Each output side is capped at 8192 pixels because browser canvases fail above that.
JPEG flattens alpha onto the page surface; choose PNG or WebP to keep it.
Very large canvases can be slow or fail on memory-constrained devices.
page.faqs:
Are my images uploaded?::No. The file is decoded and drawn on a canvas inside this tab, and the output blob is created by that same page. Nothing is sent to a server. Closing the tab discards the image, and the download is assembled locally through a temporary object URL.
What does unlocked aspect ratio do?::Unlocked mode preserves the source ratio and fits it inside both numbers you enter. A 1600 by 1200 photo asked for 800 by 800 becomes 800 by 600. Choose the width or height lock when a particular dimension must be exact.
Why is quality disabled for PNG?::PNG uses lossless compression, so a quality value would not change the encoded bytes. The slider is disabled and the hint says why. Switch to JPEG or WebP if you want a smaller file and are willing to trade a little detail for compression.
What happens to transparent pixels?::PNG and WebP keep the alpha channel, so transparent areas stay transparent. JPEG cannot store alpha, so the tool fills the canvas with the page surface before drawing. If a transparent background matters, choose PNG or WebP in the result pane.
Why was my image rejected?::Only JPEG, PNG and WebP files up to 20 MB are accepted because the browser has to decode them in memory. Convert other formats first or compress a very large photo. If a valid file still fails, re-save it from your image editor.
Can I make a huge poster-size image?::Width and height are capped at 8192 pixels per side. Browsers enforce canvas limits that vary by device, so a very large output can fail even below that number. For print-sized artwork, use desktop software with a larger canvas budget.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Output comes from the browser's canvas encoder at the format and quality you pick in the result pane, with no upload step. Updated 25 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Remove Duplicate Lines tool?
page.whatIs:
A remove duplicate lines tool scans a list one row at a time and keeps a single copy of each distinct entry. It does not rewrite your words. It only decides which rows survive, then returns the survivors in a predictable order so you can paste the result into a spreadsheet, form, script or document.

Most lists arrive from copied spreadsheets, log files or form exports, where the same value appears several times. Deduplicating by hand is slow and easy to get wrong, especially when a list has hundreds of rows. The tool compares a key for each row, and the first or last row with that key wins. Choosing Keep first preserves the earliest position, which suits signup lists. Choosing Keep last preserves the newest entry, which suits a log where the latest value matters.

Two options change what counts as the same row. Case sensitive treats Apple and apple as different entries, which is right for code, identifiers and product codes; turning it off treats them as one. Trim whitespace removes leading and trailing spaces and tabs from both the comparison and the output, so a row pasted with a stray space no longer creates a second entry. Blank lines are treated as real rows, so repeated empty lines collapse to one.

Everything runs in the browser. The result pane shows the cleaned text, the original line count, the unique line count and how many rows were removed. You can copy the text or download it as a .txt file. Real line breaks are used, so a long row that wraps on screen is still one line. Very large inputs are capped with a friendly error rather than freezing the tab.
page.howToTitle: How to use Remove Duplicate Lines
page.howTo:

Choose Keep first or Keep last under Cleanup options.
Turn on Case sensitive or Trim whitespace to match your data.

Copy the result or download it as a .txt file.

page.mistakes:
Leaving case sensitivity on::Apple and apple are different rows when the switch is on. Turn it off for names that should merge.
Forgetting whitespace::A row with a trailing space looks unique until Trim whitespace is on; the switch also cleans the output.
Expecting a summary count only::The result keeps one row per distinct key, so choose Keep last when a later row should replace an earlier one.
Pasting a whole paragraph::The tool splits on line breaks, not sentences. Put one entry on each line before you clean the list.
page.limits:
Each input accepts at most 5,000 lines or 400,000 characters.
Blank lines are counted and deduplicated like any other row.
Case folding uses simple lowercase mapping, not locale-aware rules.

page.faqs:
Which copy of a repeated line is kept?::The Keep first and Keep last tabs decide this. Keep first leaves the earliest row in its original position; Keep last moves the surviving row to where the final copy appeared. Both options preserve the order of the rows that remain, so the result stays close to your source list.
Does case sensitivity change what counts as a duplicate?::Yes. With Case sensitive on, Apple and apple are two distinct rows, which is useful for codes and identifiers. Turn it off and both are lowercased for comparison only; the output still shows the original spelling of the row that survives.
What does Trim whitespace do?::It removes leading and trailing spaces and tabs from every row before comparison and from the cleaned output. A row pasted with one extra space will no longer look unique. Spacing inside a row stays exactly as it was, so words and separators are untouched.
Are blank lines removed?::Repeated blank lines collapse to a single empty row, because an empty string is compared like any other line. A single blank line is kept, which lets you preserve a visual break between groups. Use a text editor if you want every blank row gone.
Is my text uploaded?::No. Splitting, comparison and export all happen inside your browser tab. Your list is never sent to a server, stored in an account or written to local storage. Only the option switches are remembered on this device; close the tab and the text is gone.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Sort Text Lines tool?
page.whatIs:
A sort text lines tool reorders the rows of a pasted list and leaves the text of each row unchanged. It is the fastest way to put names, tasks, product codes or log entries into a predictable order before you paste them somewhere else.

Ascending order runs from the start of the alphabet toward the end; descending reverses that. The comparison uses the characters in each row, so punctuation and spaces can affect placement. A blank line sorts to the top in ascending order because an empty string comes before any character.

Plain lexicographic sorting compares one character at a time, which puts item10 before item2 because 1 comes before 2. Natural sorting splits each row into text and digit runs and compares digit runs by value, so item2 comes before item10. This matters for file names, version labels, chapter numbers and any list that mixes words with numbers.

Case handling is the other choice. With Case sensitive on, uppercase letters sort before lowercase ones in a plain character comparison, so Cherry and cherry may sit apart. Turn it off and both are compared as lowercase while the original spelling is kept in the output. Equal rows keep their original order, and every row survives the sort.

The tool runs in the browser and caps very large inputs with a friendly error. The result pane shows the sorted text and the line count, and you can copy the text or download it as a .txt file.

Using plain sort for numbered rows::item10 jumps ahead of item2 unless Numeric (natural) sort is on.
Assuming capitals are merged::Case sensitive on keeps Cherry and cherry apart. Turn it off to compare lowercase forms.
Forgetting one entry per line::The tool sorts line breaks, not words inside a row. Put each value on its own line first.
Expecting blank lines to vanish::They sort to the top in ascending order. Remove them first if you need a gap-free list.

page.faqs:
What is the difference between plain and natural sorting?::Plain sorting compares characters one by one, so item10 appears before item2 because 1 comes first. Natural sorting splits rows into text and number runs, then compares numbers by value, giving item2 before item10. Use natural mode for file names, versions and numbered headings.
Where do blank lines go?::An empty row comes before any character, so blank lines collect at the top in ascending order and at the bottom in descending order. They are never deleted. Remove empty rows in your source text first if you want a gap-free list.
How does case sensitivity affect the result?::With Case sensitive on, capital letters sort before lowercase ones, so Cherry and cherry may sit apart. Turn it off and both rows are compared as lowercase while the original spelling is kept in the output. Equal rows keep their source order either way.

page.whatIsTitle: What is Find and Replace Text?
page.whatIs:
A find and replace tool locates every occurrence of a search term in a piece of text and writes a new value in its place. This one runs in your browser and shows a live match count before you copy or download the result.

In literal mode the search text is escaped, so a full stop, asterisk or dollar sign matches the character you typed rather than a regex instruction. In regex mode the same field is compiled as a JavaScript regular expression using the ECMAScript rules implemented by your browser. Character classes such as \d, quantifiers such as +, anchors such as ^, and lookbehind where supported all behave as they do in JavaScript. Replacement templates also follow JavaScript rules: $& inserts the whole match, $1 inserts the first capture group, and $$ writes a literal dollar sign. Literal mode escapes dollar signs for you, so currency values stay exactly as typed.

The case sensitive switch adds or removes the i flag. Whole word wraps the search in Unicode word boundaries, which prevents cat from matching category but may not isolate a term that begins with a symbol. Regex patterns are always global, so every hit is replaced rather than just the first. A pattern that can match empty text advances one character at a time, which avoids an infinite loop but can produce a large number of tiny edits.

The tool caps input at 200,000 characters and stops after 2,000 matches so the page stays responsive. Very broad patterns on long passages can still take a moment, so narrow them before running a large edit. Nothing is uploaded: the pattern, the replacement and your text stay inside this tab.

page.features:
Literal or regex::Search plain text or switch on regex mode for patterns, classes and anchors.
Case and word bounds::Toggle case sensitivity and whole-word matching for precise edits.
Live match count::Every edit refreshes the number of hits and the highlighted preview.

page.mistakes:
Forgetting to escape symbols::In literal mode symbols are escaped for you; in regex mode escape dots, brackets and plus signs yourself.
Using whole word with punctuation::Word boundaries work best on letters and digits, so check the preview when a term begins with a symbol.
Expecting unlimited scanning::Input is capped at 200,000 characters and the tool stops after 2,000 matches to keep typing responsive.

page.faqs:
Does this change my original text?::No. The tool builds a new string in your browser and leaves the text in the input box untouched. The highlighted preview shows exactly what would be copied or downloaded, so you can compare both versions before you paste the result somewhere else.
How do I replace a literal dot or dollar sign?::Leave regex mode off. Literal mode escapes every special character for you, so a dot matches a full stop and a dollar sign matches the currency symbol. The replacement text is escaped too, which means dollar signs and backslashes appear exactly as you typed them in the result.
What does whole word mean here?::Whole word adds Unicode word boundaries around your search, so cat matches the animal but not category or concatenate. It works well for ordinary words and identifiers. A term that starts or ends with punctuation may still appear inside larger strings, so check the preview before copying.
Can I use capture groups in the replacement?::Yes, in regex mode. Write groups with parentheses in the Find field, then use $1, $2 or $& in the replacement to insert them. The tool follows JavaScript replacement token rules, and $$ writes a literal dollar sign. Literal mode keeps those tokens as plain text.
Why do I see an invalid pattern error?::Regex mode compiles your search with the JavaScript RegExp engine. An unclosed bracket, a stray backslash or a quantifier with nothing before it will fail to compile. The panel shows a fix hint; adjust the pattern or switch regex mode off to search for the exact characters.
Is my text uploaded anywhere?::No. Searching, replacing and highlighting all run locally in this browser tab. The text, your search pattern and the replacement are never sent to a server, and only your switch choices are remembered on this device for the next visit.
page.trustBody: Runs on the browser's JavaScript RegExp engine, escapes literal searches and caps very long inputs. Reviewed 26 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Character Frequency Counter?
page.whatIs:
A character frequency counter reads a passage and reports how many times each character appears, usually ranked from most common to least common. This tool also shows each character's share of the total, expressed as a percentage, so you can compare short and long samples fairly.

Counting works on Unicode code points rather than raw bytes. That means a character outside the basic multilingual plane, such as an astral symbol, is counted once instead of being split into two surrogate halves. The ignore case switch folds letters to lowercase before counting, so A and a merge into one row. The ignore spaces switch skips whitespace, which is otherwise often the most frequent item in a paragraph. Punctuation is excluded by default and can be included with a switch; the rule follows the Unicode punctuation category used by modern JavaScript engines.

The rows are sorted by count, with ties resolved by the character itself. Percentages are rounded to one decimal place, so small samples may show a total that differs slightly from one hundred because of rounding. Emoji made from several code points, including joiner sequences, can appear as more than one row because each code point is counted separately.

Frequency counts are useful for spotting repeated symbols, checking keyboard layouts, teaching basic statistics and exploring simple substitution ciphers in text. Everything happens inside your browser, and your passage is never uploaded.
page.howToTitle: How to use Character Frequency Counter
page.howTo:

page.features:
Unicode code points::Each code point is counted once, so astral symbols are not split into surrogate halves.
Sorted by count::The most frequent characters come first, with ties resolved by the character itself.
Share of total::Every row shows a percentage rounded to one decimal place.
Flexible rules::Ignore case, skip whitespace or include punctuation with a single switch.
Local only::All counting and sorting happen inside your browser tab.
page.mistakes:
Counting spaces by accident::Turn on ignore spaces when a space would dominate the table.
Mixing upper and lower case::Leave ignore case on unless letter case matters to your analysis.
Expecting words::This tool counts characters, not words; use a word counter when you need word totals.
page.limits:
Emoji made of several code points may appear as multiple rows.
Very long inputs are capped and show a friendly error.
Case folding follows JavaScript lowercase rules for your locale.
page.faqs:
What counts as one character?::Each Unicode code point counts as one character. Ordinary letters and digits are straightforward, and astral symbols are kept whole instead of being split into two surrogate halves. A joiner emoji made from several code points may still occupy several rows. Turn on ignore case to merge uppercase and lowercase forms.
Why is Space at the top of the table?::Spaces are usually the most common character in prose. Turn on Ignore spaces to remove them from the count and reveal the next most frequent symbols. If you need to study spacing itself, leave the switch off and the table will include a labelled space row.
How are percentages worked out?::Each percentage is the character count divided by the total number of counted characters, multiplied by one hundred and rounded to one decimal place. Because of rounding, the visible shares may add up to slightly more or less than one hundred on very short samples.
Does ignoring case merge A and a?::Yes. With Ignore case on, each letter is converted to lowercase before counting, so A and a share a single row and the displayed character is the first one seen. Switch it off when the distinction matters, for example when checking capitalisation in a heading or a code identifier.
Can I use this for frequency analysis?::Yes. Sorting by count makes repeated letters and symbols easy to spot, which is useful for simple substitution puzzles, typography checks and teaching basic statistics. For serious cryptography work you would usually want letter frequencies by position and word patterns, which this character-only table does not provide.
Is my text sent to a server?::No. Counting and sorting run locally in your browser tab. Your text is never uploaded or stored on a server, and clearing the page removes it from memory. Only your switch choices are kept on this device so the tool opens with the same rules next time.
page.trustBody: Counts Unicode code points, sorts by frequency and shows each character's share of the total. Reviewed 26 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Readability Score Checker?
page.whatIs:
A Readability Score Checker turns a passage of prose into two numbers: a Flesch Reading Ease score and a Flesch-Kincaid grade level. Both come from the same two ratios, average words per sentence and average syllables per word, so you can see whether a draft reads like a short note or a dense article.

Flesch Reading Ease was published by Rudolph Flesch in the 1940s. The formula starts at 206.835, subtracts 1.015 times the average sentence length, then subtracts 84.6 times the average syllables per word. A result near 100 means very easy reading; a result near 0 means very hard reading. Many plain-English guidelines ask for a score of 60 or above.

Flesch-Kincaid grade level uses the same two ratios with different constants: 0.39 times sentence length, plus 11.8 times syllables per word, minus 15.59. The result is a US school grade estimate, not a test score. A grade of 8 suggests the vocabulary and sentence length typical of eighth-grade readers.

Counting is where estimates differ between tools. This checker treats each whitespace-separated token that contains a letter or number as one word. Sentence endings are full stops, exclamation marks, question marks and ellipses. Syllables come from a vowel-group rule: groups of vowels are counted, a trailing silent e is dropped, and a leading y acts as a vowel. Proper nouns, acronyms and technical terms can be counted differently from a dictionary, so the grade can shift by a level.

Use the two numbers as a signal, not a verdict. A passage with long but clear sentences can score low, while a choppy passage can score high. Run the check on a few paragraphs, compare revisions, and read the text aloud before you publish.
page.howToTitle: How to use Readability Score Checker
page.howTo:
Paste or type your passage into the Text to analyse box, or use the inline Paste button.
Watch the Flesch score, band badge and grade estimate refresh as you type.
Read the explanation under the score and the word, sentence and syllable counters.
Copy the report or download it as a .txt file for your notes.
page.useCases:
Editing web copy::Check a draft against an eighth-grade target before it goes live.
Teaching reading::Compare a set text with the level your class is expected to handle.
Accessibility reviews::Find dense paragraphs that tire readers on phones.
Revision checks::Rewrite a paragraph and see whether the estimate actually improves.
page.mistakes:
Treating the grade as exact::It is a formula applied to averages, not a reading test.
Trusting every syllable count::The vowel-group rule can miscount acronyms and names.
Ignoring abbreviation dots::An abbreviation ending in a full stop may look like a sentence end.
Judging one long word::One technical term rarely changes the score; the ratio of all words does.
page.limits:
Syllables come from an English vowel-group heuristic, not a dictionary lookup.
The score is clamped to 0 to 100 and the grade to 0 to 18.
Abbreviations with terminal dots can be counted as sentence endings.
Passages over 120,000 characters are rejected with an inline error.
page.faqs:
What does a Flesch Reading Ease score of 60 mean?::Sixty is the usual threshold for plain English in many style guides. It suggests the average sentence and word length are manageable for a broad audience. Read the band badge and the short explanation above the counters for context, then compare the score with a revised draft rather than treating one number as a rule.
Is the grade level the same as a school test result?::No. The Flesch-Kincaid grade is an estimate from average sentence length and syllables per word. It says nothing about a person's ability, and it does not measure content difficulty or background knowledge. Use it to compare drafts and spot dense writing, not to place a reader in a class.
Why does my syllable count differ from a dictionary?::The tool counts vowel groups with a short rule and drops a final silent e. A word such as business or area may be counted differently from a dictionary entry. Proper nouns, acronyms and numbers are treated as single beats. This is why the result is labelled an estimate.
Does punctuation affect the score?::Punctuation ends a sentence only when it is a full stop, exclamation mark, question mark or ellipsis. Commas and colons do not split sentences. An abbreviation with a final dot can be read as a sentence end, which lowers the average sentence length and can raise the score slightly.
Is my text uploaded or stored?::No. Counting, both formulas and the report all run inside your browser tab. Your passage is never sent to a server and is cleared when you refresh or close the page. Only the text you typed stays in the editor until you clear it, and downloading the report saves a plain file locally.
page.trustBody: Readability uses the published Flesch constants 206.835, 1.015 and 84.6, plus Flesch-Kincaid 0.39, 11.8 and 15.59, entirely in your browser.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an HTML Formatter?
page.whatIs:
An HTML Formatter takes a block of markup and rewrites its whitespace so nesting is visible. It does not change tags, attributes or text, and it never runs scripts. You paste a fragment, choose an indent width, and read a clean version with one tag per line.

This formatter works on tokens, not on a browser document. It recognises opening tags, closing tags, comments, doctype declarations and self-closing tags such as img and br. Each opening tag increases the indent level and each closing tag decreases it. Void elements from the HTML specification, including area, base, col, embed, hr, input, link, meta, source, track and wbr, do not add a level. Text between tags is trimmed and placed on its own line, with runs of whitespace collapsed to a single space.

The indent control offers two or four spaces per level, the two conventions most often used in style guides. Tabs are not offered, because mixed tabs and spaces are a common source of noisy diffs. Choosing four spaces simply multiplies the level by four.

The escape switch converts angle brackets and ampersands in the result into entities, so the formatted source can be shown as text inside a page or a documentation site. Escaping after formatting keeps the line breaks and indent intact. An existing entity gains another layer of escaping, which is expected when you want literal display.

Formatting is deliberately shallow. It does not repair malformed markup, reorder attributes or validate against a schema. If tags are left open, a notice appears next to the result, but the original order is preserved so you can fix the source yourself.
page.howToTitle: How to use HTML Formatter
page.howTo:
Paste HTML into the input box, or click Try sample to load a small fragment.
Choose 2 or 4 spaces with the Indent size control.
Turn on Escape existing markup if you want the tags shown as text.
Read the tag and line counts, then copy the result or download it as a .html file.
page.exampleLabel: One line in, nested lines out

Tags: 4 Lines: 6
page.exampleNote: The opening tag adds a level and its close removes it. Text sits on its own line with two spaces for each nested tag.
page.features:
2 or 4 spaces::Choose the indent width from the segmented control in the input pane.
One tag per line::Opening and closing tags move to their own line so nesting reads cleanly.
Void elements::Tags such as br, img and input keep their current level instead of adding one.
Escape switch::Turn markup into visible text with entities while keeping the indentation.
Tag and line counts::Read the two counters above the result before you copy or download.
page.mistakes:
Expecting repaired markup::The formatter re-indents text. It does not close missing tags or fix invalid nesting.
Pasting whole documents::A doctype is kept at the left edge; long pages produce long results within the character cap.
Forgetting the escape switch::Formatted output is still markup. Escape it before showing it as code on a page.
Reading the tag count as validation::The counter includes comments and doctype tokens, not a validity check.
page.limits:
Inputs over 100,000 characters are rejected with an inline error.
Whitespace inside text nodes collapses to one space.
Unclosed tags are counted and reported, but the original order is preserved.
No HTML is executed, parsed by a browser, or sent anywhere.
page.faqs:
Does the formatter run my scripts?::No. It matches tag-like text with a regular expression and rebuilds whitespace. Nothing is inserted into the page, no event handlers fire and no network request is made. Pasted HTML is treated purely as characters, so even a script tag becomes plain text in the output.
What does Escape existing markup do?::It converts angle brackets and ampersands in the formatted result into entities, so tags display as text instead of becoming real elements. Indentation and line breaks stay in place. Use it when you want to show a snippet in documentation or a blog post.
Why are br and img not indented further?::They are void elements in HTML, which means they have no closing tag and no children. Giving them a deeper level would misrepresent the structure. The formatter keeps them at the current level, alongside meta, input, link, hr and other void tags.
Can it fix broken HTML?::No. It re-indents what you paste and counts any tags left open, then shows a notice. It never invents missing closing tags or reorders attributes. Fix the source in the input box and the result rebuilds after a short pause.
Which file do I download?::The result is saved as formatted.html with a text/html type, so an editor opens it as markup. If the escape switch is on, the file contains entities and displays as literal code. Copy gives you the same text for pasting into another tool.
page.trustBody: Formatting is a token-based string pass over at most 100,000 characters. Pasted markup is never inserted into the document or executed.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a CSS Formatter?
page.whatIs:
A CSS Formatter rewrites a stylesheet into a consistent, indented layout without changing what the browser does. It keeps selectors, declarations, comments and strings intact, adds line breaks after braces and semicolons, and indents nested blocks so the structure of each rule is visible at a glance.

Formatting is cosmetic. The CSS Object Model treats whitespace the same whether a rule sits on one line or ten, so the cascade, specificity and source order still decide which declaration wins. Two indentation conventions dominate: two spaces per nesting level, common in JavaScript toolchains, and four spaces, common in older style guides. The indent control here offers both.

The formatter reads CSS as tokens rather than raw text. It tracks quoted strings, so a semicolon or brace inside a string never splits a declaration, and it tracks comments, so a note stays where you wrote it. Braces open and close rule blocks, while semicolons end declarations. At-rules such as @media, @supports and @keyframes nest the same way as ordinary selectors.

The property-per-line switch controls density. With it on, each declaration gets its own line, which suits reviews and long value lists. With it off, declarations in a rule share one line, which is compact but harder to scan. Rule and declaration counters update beside the output, and the result can be copied or saved as a .css file.

page.howTo:

Choose two or four spaces in the Indent control.

Read the formatted stylesheet and check the rule and property counters.
Copy the CSS or download it as a .css file.
page.features:
String-aware tokenizer::Quotes, escapes and comments are respected, so a semicolon or brace inside a string never breaks a declaration.
Two indent widths::Switch between two and four spaces per nesting level to match the style guide your team already uses.
Density control::Put every declaration on its own line, or keep short rules on one line for a tighter stylesheet.
Rule and property counts::See how many blocks and declarations the formatter found before you copy the result.
Local formatting::The stylesheet is parsed and rebuilt inside the browser; nothing is uploaded or stored.
page.mistakes:
Assuming behaviour changes::Formatting only adjusts whitespace. Specificity and source order still decide the winning declaration.
Editing minified-only source::A single-line file has no helpful breaks; paste it here before hunting for a typo.
Expecting autofix::Unbalanced braces are reported as an error, not silently repaired, so check the original CSS.
Forgetting the density switch::If declarations stay on one line, turn on One property per line before copying.
page.limits:
Inputs over 200,000 characters are rejected with a friendly message.
Unbalanced braces stop formatting until the source is corrected.
Comments are preserved verbatim, including their original line breaks.
Strings are never rewritten, so colour values inside quotes stay exactly as typed.
page.faqs:
Does formatting change how my CSS works?::No. Formatting only changes whitespace and line breaks. The browser parses the same tokens either way, so specificity, source order and the cascade still decide which declaration wins. The formatter preserves strings and comments, and it reports unbalanced braces instead of guessing at a fix.
Why do I get an unbalanced braces error?::Each opening brace must have a matching closing brace. The formatter stops when a block is left open or a closing brace appears with no opener, because guessing where a rule ends could silently change your stylesheet. Find the stray brace in the source, then paste the corrected CSS again.
What does one property per line do?::It expands each declaration onto its own indented line, which makes long value lists and reviews easier to scan. Turn it off to keep the declarations of a short rule together on one line. The choice is a layout preference only and never changes the cascade or the computed style.
Are comments and strings preserved?::Yes. The tokenizer reads quoted strings as single units, so a semicolon or brace inside a string never starts a new rule. Comments stay where you wrote them, including their text. Colours and functions inside quotes are not rewritten, and the rule and property counts ignore comment content.
Can I copy or download the result?::Yes. Copy puts the formatted stylesheet on your clipboard, and Download saves the same text as a .css file. Both buttons use the output currently shown, so set the indent width and density first. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl/Cmd plus Shift plus C copies from anywhere in the tool.
Is my stylesheet uploaded anywhere?::No. Tokenising, indentation, counting and export all run inside your browser tab. Your CSS is never sent to a server, and refreshing the page clears it. Only the indent and density choices are remembered on this device, so the stylesheet itself is not saved in local storage.
page.trustBody: This formatter tokenises CSS with quoted strings and comments protected, then rebuilds nested blocks at the chosen indent. Rules and declarations are counted from the same token stream. Formatting runs locally in your browser.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a CSS Minifier?
page.whatIs:
A CSS Minifier removes bytes the browser does not need while leaving the rendered result unchanged. It collapses runs of whitespace, deletes comments when asked, drops the final semicolon in a rule and shortens compatible colour values. Selectors, declarations and at-rules keep their original order.

Minification is not compression. Whitespace removal saves a modest share of a stylesheet, while gzip or Brotli applied by the server removes far more because repeated text compresses well. A minifier still earns its place: it shrinks the file before those encodings and strips developer notes that would otherwise ship to visitors.

This minifier scans CSS as tokens, not arbitrary text. Quoted strings are copied byte for byte, so a semicolon or brace inside a value survives. Comments are removed only when the strip comments switch is on. Colour compaction shortens six-digit hex pairs such as #ffffff to #fff and rewrites simple rgb values to hex, but never touches quotes.

Spacing follows CSS token rules. Spaces around braces, semicolons, commas and combinators can go, while one space between two words must stay so that div span does not become divspan. The size panel reports the original length, the minified length and the percentage saved, and the result can be copied or saved as a .min.css file.
page.howToTitle: How to use CSS Minifier

page.features:
Whitespace pass::Collapses spacing outside strings and comments, then drops optional semicolons before a closing brace.
Comment control::Strip comments removes notes from the output; leaving it off keeps them.
Colour compaction::Shortens paired hex digits and simple rgb values without changing colours.
Size comparison::Original bytes, minified bytes and the saved percentage sit next to the result.

page.mistakes:
Expecting gzip levels::Minification removes redundant characters, not repeated text; server compression still does the heavy lifting.
Stripping important comments::License notices inside normal comments disappear when Strip comments is on, so keep those in a separate file.
Worrying about strings::Quoted values are copied unchanged, so a brace inside a string cannot break the output.
Comparing against source maps::Minified CSS has no source map here; keep the readable stylesheet for debugging.

page.faqs:
Does minification change the design?::No. The minifier removes characters the parser does not need, such as repeated spaces and the final semicolon in a rule. Selectors, declarations and at-rules keep their order, and quoted strings are copied unchanged. Colour compaction shortens only values that represent the same colour.
How is the saved percentage calculated?::It is one minus the minified character count divided by the original character count, rounded to a whole percent. The two size counters show the numbers behind it. Because the math uses characters, gzip or Brotli savings will be different and usually larger.
What does compact colours do?::It shortens six-digit hex colours whose channels repeat in pairs, so #ffffff becomes #fff and #112233cc becomes #123c. It also rewrites simple rgb values with integer channels into hex. Named colours, rgba values and any colour inside a quoted string are left exactly as written.
Are strings and comments safe?::Quoted strings are copied byte for byte, so a semicolon or brace inside content cannot break the output. Comments are removed only when Strip comments is on. Whitespace is collapsed outside strings and comments, which keeps selectors like div span distinct from divspan.
Why would I keep comments in minified CSS?::License notices and build markers sometimes need to ship with the file. Leaving Strip comments off keeps them while whitespace is still compacted. For production, turning it on gives the smallest output, so keep legal notices in a separate file if you need both.
Can I copy or download the result?::Yes. Copy places the minified stylesheet on your clipboard, and Download saves the same text as a .min.css file. Both actions use the current settings, so choose the comment and colour options first. The shortcut Ctrl/Cmd plus Shift plus C also copies the result.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a JS Minifier?
page.whatIs:
JS Minifier is a browser tool that reduces a JavaScript file to fewer characters while keeping the program's behaviour intact. It works by tokenising the source into words, numbers, strings, template literals, regular expressions, comments and operators, then joining the significant tokens with only the whitespace that is still required. Because it never evaluates the input, your code is never executed.

Comment stripping is the largest and safest saving. A line comment is dropped entirely and a block comment is dropped entirely, but any line break inside a removed comment is remembered so automatic semicolon insertion still behaves the same way. String contents, template interpolations and regex bodies are treated as opaque text, so a double slash inside a URL or a slash and star inside a pattern is never mistaken for a comment.

Whitespace is removed only when two adjacent tokens cannot merge. A space stays between two identifiers, between a number and a leading dot, or between two plus or minus signs that would otherwise become increment or decrement operators. A space also stays where a slash could start a comment. Newlines that follow return, throw, break, continue or a postfix increment are replaced with an explicit semicolon, which preserves the same statement boundaries after the output is collapsed onto fewer lines.

The preserve-semicolons switch controls the last safe reduction. With it off, the minifier drops semicolons that are redundant before a closing brace, at the end of a file, or next to an empty statement, but keeps the separators that for headers and protective leading semicolons need.

Size is reported in UTF-8 bytes for both the pasted source and the result, and the saved percent is derived from those two numbers. Multi-byte characters and surrogate pairs are counted correctly.
page.howToTitle: How to use JS Minifier
page.howTo:
Paste or type JavaScript into the source box, or use the inline Paste button.
Toggle Strip comments to remove or keep line and block comments.
Toggle Preserve semicolons to keep all statement separators.
Read the original bytes, minified bytes and saved percent under the result.
Copy the minified code or download it as a .min.js file.
page.features:
Comment aware::Line and block comments are recognised outside strings, templates and regexes.
Safe whitespace::Spaces are removed only where tokens cannot merge or change meaning.
Semicolon control::Keep every semicolon or drop only the redundant ones.
Real size stats::Original and minified UTF-8 byte counts plus the saved percent.
Private by design::The source is tokenised in the browser and never evaluated or uploaded.
page.mistakes:
Expecting name mangling::This tool shortens whitespace and comments only. Variable and function names stay unchanged.
Minifying broken input::An unterminated string, template or comment reports an error instead of guessing.
Pasting minified code again::Running the tool twice adds no extra saving. Start from the readable source.
Assuming smaller always wins::Some environments need the original stack traces, so keep a copy before shipping.
page.limits:
Input is capped at 500,000 characters; shorten the file if the cap error appears.
Identifier names are not renamed and no dead code is removed.
Whitespace inside strings, templates and regex literals is preserved verbatim.
Semicolon removal is conservative: separators needed by for headers stay in place.
page.faqs:
Does the minifier run my JavaScript?::No. The source is read as text and split into tokens, then the tokens are joined back together. Nothing is evaluated, compiled or executed, so a script with side effects cannot run while you minify it.
Why are some spaces kept?::Removing the wrong space can merge two tokens or change a statement. A space stays between identifiers, around double signs, before a dot after a number and anywhere a slash could begin a comment.
What does Preserve semicolons change?::With the switch off, only semicolons that are redundant before a closing brace, at the end of the file or beside an empty statement are dropped. With it on, every semicolon in the source is kept.
How is the saved percent calculated?::Both the original and the result are counted as UTF-8 bytes, including multi-byte characters and surrogate pairs. The saved percent is one minus the result count divided by the original count, rounded to the nearest whole number.
Will it work with TypeScript or JSX?::It treats unknown syntax as ordinary tokens, so many modern constructs pass through, but TypeScript types and JSX tags are not parsed. Use compiled JavaScript for predictable results, especially before type annotations or JSX attributes.
page.trustBody: The minifier tokenises source without executing it, keeps whitespace that matters for automatic semicolon insertion, and counts both sizes in UTF-8 bytes.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a SQL Formatter?
page.whatIs:
SQL Formatter is a browser tool that turns a dense query into readable text without changing what the query does. It reads the input as tokens rather than executing it, so quoted strings, quoted identifiers, dollar-quoted blocks and comments pass through unchanged. Formatting only changes whitespace, indentation and the case of unquoted keywords.

The formatter splits statements on semicolons that sit outside strings and comments, then breaks each major clause onto its own line. Select lists, where conditions, group by, order by, join and on clauses each start a new line, while and and or continue one level deeper. Commas at the top level also start a new line, which makes long column lists easy to scan. Parenthesised expressions stay on one line so functions such as count(*) keep their shape.

Keyword casing is a display choice. With uppercase keywords enabled, words in the SQL keyword set are printed in capitals while single-quoted values, double-quoted identifiers, backtick names and bracket names keep the exact characters you typed. With the switch off, original casing is preserved, which suits teams whose style guide prefers lower case.

The indent control offers two or four spaces and applies to continuation lines only. Clause keywords begin at the left margin in both modes. Statement and line counters update with the formatted text, and the result can be copied or saved as a .sql file. Because tokenising happens locally, a query containing credentials never leaves the tab.
page.howToTitle: How to use SQL Formatter
page.howTo:
Paste or type a query into the SQL box, or use the inline Paste button.
Choose two or four spaces in the indent control under the result.
Toggle Uppercase keywords to match your team's SQL style.
Read the formatted query and its statement and line counts.
Copy the result or download it as a .sql file.
page.exampleInput: select id,name from users where active=1 order by name;
page.exampleOutput:
SELECT
  id,
  name
FROM users
WHERE active = 1
ORDER BY name;
page.exampleNote: The comma inside the select list starts a new indented line, while each clause begins at the left margin. Strings and quoted names are never altered.
page.mistakes:
Editing inside strings::Quoted values and identifiers are copied exactly as typed, so changing case there is a real data change.
Expecting validation::This tool formats text and does not check tables, columns or syntax against a database.
Splitting a comment::A line comment ends at the newline, so the next clause starts after it. Keep notes on their own line.
Forgetting the dialect::Dollar-quoted blocks and bracket names are handled, but some vendor-specific syntax stays as typed.
page.limits:
Input is capped at 300,000 characters.
Keywords are matched from a built-in list; unknown dialect words keep their original case.
No query is sent to a database or checked for correctness.
Long single-line comments are not wrapped automatically.
page.faqs:
Does the formatter connect to my database?::No. It reads the query as plain text and rewrites whitespace and keyword case only. There is no connection, no schema lookup and no validation of table or column names, so the same query formats the same way whether or not the database exists.
Why did my string value keep its lower case?::Quoted text is data, not syntax. Single-quoted values, double-quoted identifiers, backtick names and bracket names are copied character for character, even when Uppercase keywords is on. This prevents a formatter from changing a password, label or column name.
What changes when I switch from two to four spaces?::Only continuation lines move. Clause keywords begin at the left margin in both modes, while select items, condition lines and comma-separated entries shift by the chosen indent. The statement text itself is identical, so you can switch freely.
How are statement and line counts calculated?::A statement ends at a semicolon outside strings and comments, and any trailing text without a semicolon counts as one more statement. Line count is the number of lines in the formatted result, including blank lines between statements.
Can it format more than one query at a time?::Yes. Paste a script with several statements and each one is laid out in turn, separated by a blank line. Unterminated strings or block comments are reported as errors with a hint to fix the source before formatting.
page.trustBody: The formatter tokenises queries locally, keeps quoted text verbatim and breaks clauses onto separate lines without checking them against a database.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Cron Expression Generator?
page.whatIs:
A cron expression generator turns a human schedule into the five-field string that a cron daemon reads. The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, in that order. There is no seconds field in the classic format and no year field. Each field accepts a single value, a comma-separated list, a hyphenated range or a step such as */5. Three-letter names are valid for month and weekday fields. Weekday zero and seven both mean Sunday.

The tool parses each field against its own limits: minutes run from 0 to 59, hours from 0 to 23, days from 1 to 31, months from 1 to 12 and weekdays from 0 to 7. It rejects an empty field, a value outside its range, a reversed range, a zero step and a name used in the wrong place. Valid fields are rewritten into one canonical expression, so spaces are tidied, lists are sorted and weekday seven becomes zero.

When both the day of month and day of week fields are restricted, common cron implementations match either one, not both. This tool follows that rule and says so in the explanation. The next-run preview scans minute by minute for one year using the device clock, so it reflects local time rather than a server timezone.

Nothing is sent anywhere. Parsing, validation, the plain-English sentence and the preview all run in the browser, and a copy or download keeps the expression together with its meaning.

Copy the expression or download it as a text file.

hour 9

month *
weekday 1-5

Runs every Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday at 09:00.
page.exampleNote: The next-run list is calculated from your device clock when the page loads, so it will not match a fixed date here.
page.features:
Five-field parser::Each field is checked against its own minute, hour, day, month or weekday limits.
Canonical output::Values are sorted and tidied into one copyable expression.
Plain English::A short sentence describes the schedule without cron jargon.
Next-run preview::Up to three upcoming times are shown from your device clock.
Local only::No expression is uploaded and no account is needed.
page.mistakes:
Thinking the first field is a second::Classic cron starts with minute. There is no seconds field here.
Using both day fields by accident::When day of month and day of week are both set, cron matches either one.
Forgetting the timezone::The preview uses your device clock, so a server schedule may run at a different local time.
Assuming a name works everywhere::Use numbers for the widest compatibility, even though JAN and MON are accepted.
page.limits:
No seconds or year field is supported.
The next-run preview stops after one year.
A schedule rarer than once a year may show fewer than three upcoming times.
page.faqs:
What do the five fields mean?::They are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, in that order. Minute runs from 0 to 59, hour from 0 to 23, day from 1 to 31, month from 1 to 12 and weekday from 0 to 7. Zero and seven both mean Sunday.
Can I use names such as MON or JAN?::Yes. Three-letter names work in the month and weekday fields, and they are not case sensitive. The canonical expression rewrites them as numbers, which keeps the result readable in tools that do not accept names. Names are rejected in the minute, hour and day fields because they have no meaning there.
Why does my job still run many times on a weekday?::If a field still contains an asterisk it places no restriction on that part of the schedule. A weekday value alone does not limit the hour or minute, so the job may fire repeatedly that day. Set the hour and minute fields as well, or use one of the presets.
How far ahead does the next-run preview look?::It scans minute by minute for one year from the moment the page calculates it. That covers annual schedules, but a date such as 29 February may show fewer than three results in a year without that day. Times come from your device clock, so check the server timezone separately.
Is my schedule stored anywhere?::No. The five fields live only in this browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no sign-in, and the copy and download actions read the expression from the page. Closing the tab clears what you typed.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an HMAC Generator?
page.whatIs:
An HMAC generator computes a keyed hash message authentication code: a short digest that proves a message was created by someone who knows a shared secret. Unlike a plain hash, an HMAC needs two inputs, the message and a secret key, so changing either one changes the output completely. The scheme is standardised in RFC 2104 and is widely used to sign API requests, verify webhook payloads and protect session tokens.

This tool uses the HMAC implementation built into the Web Crypto API. You can choose SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512 as the underlying hash. SHA-256 returns 256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters, while SHA-512 returns 512 bits or 128 characters. SHA-1 returns 160 bits or 40 characters, but published collision attacks make it a poor choice for new security work. It is included only for legacy systems that still expect a 40 character tag.

Both the message and the secret are encoded as UTF-8 before signing. A trailing space, a different line ending or a different encoding changes the bytes and therefore the tag. An empty message or an empty secret produces no result here, because a tag without a real key has little practical value. Once both fields contain text, the digest updates after a short pause while you type.

A keyed digest confirms integrity and authenticity only when the secret is genuinely private. Anyone who learns the secret can forge a valid tag, so use a long random key and never place it in a public page or a client side script that untrusted users can read. On the server, compare tags in constant time to avoid timing leaks. This tool computes tags locally and never transmits either input, but it does not verify signatures or manage keys for you.
page.howToTitle: How to use HMAC Generator
page.howTo:
Type or paste a message into the message box.
Enter a secret key in the secret field.
Choose SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512 in the segmented control.
Switch on Uppercase digest near the result if you need capital hex characters.

page.features:
Three hash choices::Sign with SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512 from the Web Crypto API.
Live keyed tags::The digest updates after a short pause and stale requests are discarded.
Casing switch::Toggle uppercase hex near the result without recomputing the tag.
Exact sizes::See the tag length in bits and bytes for the selected algorithm.
Private by design::Message and secret stay in the browser tab and are never uploaded.
page.mistakes:
Using a short secret::A guessable key makes forged tags easy. Use a long random value kept only on trusted systems.
Choosing SHA-1 for new work::Known collision attacks make it unsuitable for signatures. Pick SHA-256 or SHA-512.
Confusing HMAC with encryption::A tag proves authenticity, not secrecy. The message itself is still readable.
Comparing tags with a normal string check::On a server, use a constant time comparison to avoid timing leaks.
page.limits:
Each field is capped at 100,000 characters so signing stays responsive.
Web Crypto needs HTTPS or localhost; plain HTTP pages cannot compute HMAC.
Both a message and a secret are required before a tag is shown.
This tool computes tags only. It does not verify signatures or store secrets.
page.faqs:
Is my message or secret uploaded anywhere?::No. Both values are read by the Web Crypto API inside your browser tab, and nothing is sent to a server, logged or stored. Closing the page discards them. Use a trusted page when working with real production secrets.
What is the difference between a hash and an HMAC?::A plain hash accepts one input and anyone can recompute it. An HMAC also takes a secret key, so only someone who knows that key can produce the same tag. That makes it suitable for authenticating messages, not just detecting accidental changes.
Which algorithm should I choose?::SHA-256 is a good default and produces a 64 character tag. SHA-512 gives a longer 128 character tag when a protocol asks for it. SHA-1 is available for legacy systems only, because researchers have demonstrated practical collision attacks against it.
Why is there no result when one field is empty?::An HMAC with no message or no real key has little practical value, so the tool keeps the result pane empty until both fields contain text. Add a message and a secret, and the digest appears after a brief pause.
Can I uppercase the digest?::Yes. The Uppercase switch sits next to the result and changes only how the hexadecimal tag is displayed and copied. It does not change the underlying bytes, so uppercase and lowercase forms of the same tag are equivalent.
Does this work on every browser?::It needs a secure context, meaning HTTPS or localhost, because Web Crypto's subtle API is hidden on ordinary HTTP pages. Current Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge support HMAC with all three SHA algorithms listed here.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Tags come from the browser's Web Crypto API using RFC 2104 HMAC with SHA-1, SHA-256 or SHA-512. Last updated 26 November 2026.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Random String Generator?
page.whatIs:
A random string generator creates a sequence of characters that an attacker cannot predict. This tool draws every character from the browser's crypto.getRandomValues API, which is backed by the operating system's cryptographically secure random source. There is no Math.random fallback, so the output is suitable for tokens, test credentials, sample identifiers and one time secrets.

You control the length, from four to one hundred twenty eight characters, and the batch count, up to one hundred strings per run. Four character sets are available: lowercase letters, uppercase letters, digits and symbols. Selecting more sets widens the pool and raises the number of possible strings. The generator draws uniformly from the combined pool and uses rejection sampling so a plain modulo operation cannot favour the first characters.

The exclude look-alikes switch removes i, l, one, I, L, o, O and zero from the pool. That makes strings easier to read aloud or retype from a screen, though it slightly reduces the number of available characters. Symbols include punctuation such as exclamation marks and brackets, which some systems reject, so turn that set off when a destination accepts only letters and digits.

Each string in a batch is independent, and no string is stored or sent anywhere. Generation happens when you press the button, not while you type, so the result stays stable until you ask for a new batch. For real passwords, prefer a long string with several character sets, and store the result in a password manager rather than reusing it across sites.
page.howToTitle: How to use Random String Generator
page.howTo:
Set the string length with the number stepper.
Set the batch count for how many strings to create.
Tick the lowercase, uppercase, digit and symbol sets you want.
Switch on Exclude look-alikes if the strings will be read or typed by hand.
Press Generate, then copy the batch or download it as a .txt file.
page.featuresTitle: What this Random String Generator does
page.features:
Secure source::Every character comes from crypto.getRandomValues, with no Math.random fallback.
Uniform draws::Rejection sampling avoids the small bias a plain modulo would introduce.
Flexible sets::Mix lowercase, uppercase, digits and symbols to fit the destination.
Look-alike control::Drop confusing characters when values will be read aloud or retyped.
Batches and export::Create up to one hundred strings at once, then copy or save a .txt file.
page.mistakes:
Using Math.random for secrets::It is predictable and is never used here. Keep generated values out of client side code that exposes them.
Turning off every set::No characters remain, so the Generate button is disabled until a set is selected.
Assuming longer always means stronger::Length helps, but a small character pool and reused values weaken security.
Including symbols where they are rejected::Some systems accept only letters and digits, so untick symbols for those fields.
page.limits:
Length is limited to 4 through 128 characters and a batch to at most 100 strings.
The browser must provide crypto.getRandomValues; there is no insecure fallback.
Excluding look-alikes removes characters from every selected set, reducing variety slightly.
Strings are generated on demand and are not saved after you close the page.
page.faqs:
Is this random enough for passwords?::Yes for most everyday uses. Every character comes from crypto.getRandomValues, the same secure source browsers provide for TLS and key generation. There is no Math.random fallback. Use a long string, keep it unique per site, and store it in a password manager.
What does exclude look-alikes do?::It removes letters and digits that are easy to confuse, such as lower case l, upper case I and the digit one, plus o, O and zero. Strings stay unpredictable but are easier to read aloud or retype from a screen, at the cost of a slightly smaller pool.
How many strings can I make at once?::A batch can hold between one and one hundred strings, and each string can be four to one hundred twenty eight characters long. Increase the batch count with the number stepper, then press Generate. Copy the whole batch or save it as a .txt file.
Are the strings sent anywhere?::No. Generation happens entirely in your browser tab and nothing is uploaded, logged or stored. The values exist only in the result pane until you navigate away or press Generate again. Avoid pasting real secrets into tools you do not trust.
Why are symbols a separate option?::Punctuation characters widen the pool and raise entropy, but many forms and legacy systems reject them. Keeping symbols as an optional set lets you produce clean alphanumeric values when a destination requires them, and stronger strings when it does not.
Does the generator favour any characters?::No. The tool asks the browser for a random 32 bit integer, discards values that would bias a modulo operation, and takes the remainder. That rejection sampling keeps every character in the selected pool equally likely, even when the pool size does not divide evenly into the integer range.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Every value comes from the browser's crypto.getRandomValues API using rejection sampling for uniform picks. Last updated 26 November 2026.

page.directAnswer: Meta Tag Generator builds the head tags a search engine reads, including title, description, canonical URL, robots and theme colour. Every value is HTML escaped, and the finished tags update live so you can copy or download them as an .html file.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a meta tag generator?
page.whatIs:
A meta tag generator writes the small head elements that describe a page to browsers, crawlers and social previews. This tool turns five plain fields into a ready block of HTML: the document title, the description meta tag, the canonical link, the robots directive and the theme colour declaration. Nothing is uploaded or rendered; the output is text you can paste into the head of a page.

The title is written as a title element because search engines use it as the clickable heading in results. The description lives in a description meta tag. A search engine may show it as snippet text, though it is not a direct ranking factor and can replace it with text from the page. The canonical link names the preferred URL when the same content is reachable at more than one address, such as with tracking parameters or trailing slashes.

Robots directives tell crawlers what to do with a page. Index and follow allows both indexing and link discovery; noindex and follow hides the page while still passing signals through links; index and nofollow keeps the page indexed without following its links; noindex and nofollow blocks both. The theme colour sets the browser chrome colour on supported mobile browsers and is normally written as a hex value such as #0f172a.

Every value is escaped before it is placed in the HTML. Ampersands become the amp entity, angle brackets become the lt and gt entities, and both quote styles become entities, so a title containing a quotation mark or a description containing an ampersand cannot break out of its attribute or introduce markup. The tags stay in a stable order, update as you type, and can be copied or downloaded as an .html file.
page.howToTitle: How to use Meta Tag Generator
page.howTo:
Type the page title in the Title field, then add a short description underneath.
Paste the preferred page address into the Canonical URL field.
Choose a robots directive from the select, such as index, follow.
Add a hex theme colour if the page needs one in the browser chrome.
Copy the generated tags or download them as meta-tags.html.
page.exampleInput:
Title: Running Shoes | Northwind
Description: Lightweight running shoes with free returns and a 30 day trial.
Canonical: https://example.com/running-shoes
Robots: index, follow
Theme: #0f172a
page.exampleOutput:
<title>Running Shoes | Northwind</title>
<meta name="description" content="Lightweight running shoes with free returns and a 30 day trial.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/running-shoes">
<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#0f172a">
page.exampleNote: Values are escaped in the generated markup, so quotes and ampersands in a title cannot break the tag.
page.features:
Live head block::Title, description, canonical link, robots and theme colour appear as soon as you type.
HTML escaping::Ampersands, angle brackets and both quote styles are converted to safe entities.
Canonical support::The preferred address is written as a link element, not a meta tag.
Robots presets::Four common index and follow combinations are available from the select.
Portable output::Copy the snippet or download it as meta-tags.html for any static site or template.
page.mistakes:
Treating description as ranking fuel::The description may be rewritten in search results, so write it for readers rather than keyword density.
Forgetting a canonical URL::Duplicate pages with tracking parameters need one preferred address to consolidate signals.
Using noindex by accident::A noindex directive removes a page from search results; choose index, follow for normal pages.
Pasting raw quotes::Unescaped quotation marks can end an attribute early. The builder escapes them for you.
page.limits:
The tool writes only the five head fields shown; it does not validate search engine policies.
Long titles and descriptions are not truncated, so check how search engines display them.
Theme colour is written as entered; use a hex value for reliable browser support.
Canonical addresses are not fetched or checked for redirects.
page.faqs:
Which meta tags does this tool create?::It creates a title element, a description meta tag, a canonical link, a robots meta tag and a theme colour meta tag. Fields left blank are skipped except robots, which always uses the selected directive. The tags are emitted in that order.
Does a meta description improve rankings?::Search engines may use the description as snippet text, but it is not a direct ranking signal and can be replaced with text from the page. Write a clear summary for readers, and keep it short enough to display. This tool does not truncate it for you.
When should I use a canonical link?::Use a canonical link when one page can be reached at several addresses, for example with tracking parameters, sorting options or a trailing slash. The link names the preferred URL so search engines can consolidate duplicate signals. Paste the clean address into the canonical field.
What does the robots select change?::It writes a robots meta tag with one of four directives: index and follow, noindex and follow, index and nofollow, or noindex and nofollow. Index controls whether the page may appear in results, while follow controls whether crawlers follow its links.
Can I copy or download the generated tags?::Yes. The Copy button places the whole block on your clipboard and the Download button saves it as an HTML file. Both use the current fields, and the shortcut with Control or Command, Shift and C also copies the tags.
page.trustBody: Meta tags are assembled as plain strings in the browser. Each value is escaped before it enters an element or attribute, and the canonical address is written as a link element rather than a meta tag. No text is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
