page.faqs:
How are walking calories calculated?::The tool multiplies a MET value by your weight in kilograms and by the time in hours. Your pace sets the speed, and the speed looks up a MET from separate walking and running tables. The total is gross energy, which includes resting burn.
Can I enter time instead of distance?::Yes. Switch to duration mode and enter the number of minutes you moved. Add your usual pace, and the calculator works out the distance from time and pace, then uses the same MET table to estimate energy. The speed and distance appear in the breakdown.
Does the tool handle miles and pounds?::Yes. Choose miles for distance and pace, or pounds for weight, and the calculator converts them with standard factors before doing the arithmetic. Miles use 1.609344 kilometers each and pounds use 0.45359237 kilograms each, so the MET lookup always works in kilometers per hour.
Why is my estimate different from a watch?::Watches combine step counts, heart rate and personal data, while this tool uses only weight, pace and time. Hills, wind, surface, fitness and stride efficiency can shift real energy use by a wide margin. Use the number to compare options and plan, not as a precise reading.
page.trustBody: Walking and running estimates use published MET ranges with linear interpolation between table points. All arithmetic runs in your browser, and only your preferred units are remembered. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How Many Calories Does a Walk Burn?
page.guidance:
Walking and running calories are estimated with the MET method: energy in kcal equals MET multiplied by body weight in kilograms and time in hours. Your pace sets the speed, and the speed looks up a MET from separate walking and running tables, with values between points interpolated. A 70 kg walker at 5 km/h for 60 minutes uses a MET of 4.3 and burns about 301 kcal. That figure is gross energy, so it includes the calories you would have burned sitting still for the same hour.

Use the estimate to compare options rather than to track a precise burn. Enter either distance or minutes plus your usual pace; the calculator solves for the other value and shows speed and intensity so a brisk walk can be checked against a slow run. Hills, wind, surface and stride efficiency change real energy use more than pace alone suggests, so treat the number as a planning figure. If you are adding movement to a food budget, keep the net gain conservative because the gross figure already counts resting burn.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Recipe Serving Scaler Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A recipe serving scaler multiplies every ingredient amount by one factor so a dish fits a different number of servings. This tool reads one ingredient per line, finds a leading quantity when there is one, multiplies it and writes the new amount back in place. Text without a leading number, such as salt to taste, is copied unchanged.

You can scale in two ways. Enter the recipe's original servings and the servings you want, and the factor is desired divided by original. Or press a multiplier chip for half, single, double or triple batch. The chips set the desired servings for you, and typing a new serving count clears the chip selection.

Amounts come back as readable fractions where possible. Values near one half, one third, two thirds, one quarter, three quarters, one eighth or their common mixed forms use fraction characters. Anything that does not land near a clean fraction is shown as a decimal with at most two places. A quantity of 1.5 cups at double becomes 3 cups, while 0.5 teaspoon at triple becomes 1.5 teaspoons, shown as one and a half.

The tool only scales the first number on each line. Ranges, oven temperatures and times are not adjusted, so read the result before cooking. Pan sizes and cooking times rarely scale in a straight line, and spices often need less than a pure multiple when a recipe grows. Use the copyable recipe as a starting point and adjust by taste.

How does the scaler change ingredient amounts?::It finds the first number on each ingredient line, multiplies it by your factor and writes the result back with its original unit and text. Amounts near a clean fraction use fraction characters, while other amounts use a decimal with up to two places.
What if a line has no number?::Lines such as salt to taste or a note about preparation are copied through unchanged. The scaled list keeps the same line order as your input, so you can compare the original and the result side by side before you copy it.

Are cooking times and pan sizes scaled too?::No. Only ingredient quantities change. Cooking time, oven temperature and pan size depend on volume and surface area, so they do not scale in a straight line. Read the scaled recipe and adjust those details by experience and by watching the food.

page.guidance:
A recipe scaler resizes every ingredient by one factor so the dish fits a different yield. The tool changes only the first number on each line, keeps the unit and the rest of the text, and returns clean fractions where they land near a half, third, quarter or eighth, otherwise a decimal with two places. Lines without a leading amount, such as salt to taste, pass through unchanged.

Scaling from four servings to six gives a factor of 1.5, so 2 cups of broth becomes 3 cups and 1/2 cup of onion becomes 3/4 cup. Use the multiplier chips when you want a half, double or triple batch without typing new serving counts; typing a count clears the chip. Read the result before cooking, because oven temperature, cooking time and pan size do not change with volume, and strong spices often need less than a straight multiple when a batch grows.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Freelance Hourly Rate Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A freelance hourly rate calculator starts with the income you want to keep and works backward to a price you can charge. The core formula is: required revenue = (target net income + annual expenses) / (1 - tax and buffer rate as a decimal). Divide that revenue by your total billable hours for the year, which is billable weeks multiplied by billable hours per week, and you have a baseline hourly rate.

The daily rate takes that hourly figure and multiplies it by the hours you can bill in one day, estimated as weekly billable hours divided by billable days per week. The project rate multiplies the hourly figure by the number of hours in a typical project. Keeping all three rates tied to one hourly baseline means a day or a project never quietly undercuts your target.

Three assumptions matter. First, target net income is what you keep after expenses and tax, not gross revenue. Second, the tax and buffer field is a single combined percentage of revenue, so a rate of 25 means you set aside a quarter of every invoice. Third, billable time is not the same as working time. Admin, sales and holidays belong outside the billable count, which is why the sample uses 46 weeks and 30 hours rather than a full calendar.

The tool rounds the displayed rates to two decimal places but keeps full precision until the final step. A tax and buffer value of 100 percent or more is rejected because no revenue would remain as income. Zero billable weeks, hours or days are also rejected since they would make the division impossible. Everything runs locally in your browser.

page.features:
Hourly rate::Required annual revenue divided by total billable hours, the baseline for every other rate.
Daily rate::The hourly rate multiplied by billable hours per day, found from your weekly hours and days.
Project rate::The hourly rate multiplied by the hours you expect in one typical project.
Revenue needed::Target net income plus expenses, grossed up for tax and buffer before any division.
page.mistakes:
Using working hours instead of billable hours::Only count hours a client pays for, or the rate will be too low.
Forgetting expenses::Tools, insurance and software come out of revenue, so add them before the division.
Treating tax as a flat add on::A 25 percent set aside means revenue is divided by 0.75, not multiplied by 1.25.
Rounding the hourly rate too early::Round only the displayed figures and reuse the precise value for daily and project rates.
page.limits:
Tax and buffer must stay below 100 percent.
Billable weeks, hours per week and days per week must all be positive.
Income and expense figures are per year, while rates are shown per hour, day and project.
Displayed rates are rounded to two decimal places.
page.faqs:
How do I choose a freelance hourly rate?::Start with the income you need to keep, add yearly expenses and gross that total up for tax and savings. Divide by the hours you can realistically bill. This tool does that arithmetic and shows hourly, daily and project rates so you can quote consistently.
Why is my daily rate lower than I expected?::The daily rate uses billable hours per day, which this tool estimates from your weekly billable hours divided by billable days per week. If you bill 30 hours across five days, a day is six billable hours, not eight. Reduce the days per week to raise the daily figure.
What does the tax and buffer percentage mean?::It is one combined share of every invoice that you set aside for tax and savings. Enter 25 and the tool assumes 75 percent of revenue remains as take-home income, so required revenue is divided by 0.75. Values of 100 or more are rejected.
Should I bill by the hour, day or project?::Use the hourly rate for ongoing work, the daily rate for short engagements and the project rate for a fixed scope. All three come from the same baseline, so switching between them will not change what you earn as long as the hours are accurate.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Every rate is computed locally in your browser from the numbers you enter, with no upload and no account. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: What Should My Freelance Hourly Rate Be?
page.guidance:
A freelance hourly rate works backward from the take home income you want to keep. Add annual business expenses to that target, divide by one minus the tax and buffer percentage as a decimal, then divide the result by billable weeks times billable hours per week. The daily rate multiplies the hourly figure by hours billed per day, and the project rate multiplies it by hours in a typical project. Billable time excludes admin, sales and holidays, so using working hours as the divisor would push the rate too low.

Suppose you want a 60000 net income, spend 6000 a year on tools and insurance, and set aside 25 percent of revenue. Required revenue is 66000 divided by 0.75, or 88000. Across 46 billable weeks at 30 hours, that is 1380 hours and a rate near 63.77 per hour. If you bill six hours a day, the daily rate is about 382.61, and a 20 hour project is about 1275. Quote all three from the same baseline so a fixed price never quietly undercuts your target.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Break-Even Point Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A break-even point calculator finds the sales volume where total revenue exactly covers total costs, leaving neither profit nor loss. The formula is break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit, where contribution per unit is price per unit minus variable cost per unit. Each unit sold contributes that margin toward the costs you pay regardless of volume.

Break-even revenue is the unit count multiplied by the price per unit. This tool rounds the unit count up to a whole number, because you cannot sell a fraction of a unit, and then reports the revenue at that whole-unit count. It also shows the exact decimal unit count so you can see how close the whole number sits to the true threshold.

The contribution margin ratio is contribution per unit divided by price, written as a percentage. A price of 50 with a variable cost of 30 gives contribution of 20 and a ratio of 40 percent. You can also divide fixed costs by that ratio to estimate break-even revenue directly, which is useful when you track sales in currency rather than units.

Two cases have no break-even point. If price equals variable cost, contribution is zero and no number of sales will ever cover fixed costs. If price is below variable cost, every sale makes the gap larger. The tool explains both cases with a short message instead of showing a misleading number. All arithmetic runs locally in your browser.

Fixed costs can cover any period you choose, such as a month or a product launch. The result is expressed in the same period, so monthly fixed costs produce a monthly break-even target. Inputs must be zero or positive, and displayed money values are rounded to two decimal places while the underlying math keeps more precision.
page.exampleInput:
Fixed costs: 4000
Price per unit: 50
Variable cost per unit: 30
page.exampleOutput:
Contribution per unit: 20
Break-even units: 200
Break-even revenue: 10000
Contribution margin ratio: 40%
page.exampleNote: Each sale contributes 20 toward the 4000 in fixed costs, so exactly 200 units clear the target and bring in 10000 in revenue.
page.features:
Break-even units::Fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, rounded up to a whole unit.
Break-even revenue::Whole break-even units multiplied by the price per unit.
Contribution per unit::Price minus variable cost, the amount each sale adds toward fixed costs.
Contribution margin ratio::Contribution as a percentage of price, useful for revenue based targets.
page.mistakes:
Ignoring variable costs::Revenue alone does not cover costs, so subtract what each unit costs to make.
Using a negative contribution::A price below variable cost means every sale widens the gap, so there is no break-even point.
Rounding units down::Always round up to a whole unit, or the last partial sale will leave costs uncovered.
Mixing periods::Fixed costs, revenue and the break-even target must all refer to the same period.
page.limits:
Price and variable cost must be zero or positive, and price must exceed variable cost to return a result.
A zero or negative contribution is reported with an explanation.
Units are rounded up to the next whole number.
Money values are displayed to two decimal places.
page.faqs:
What is the break-even point?::It is the sales level where revenue equals total costs, so profit is zero. The calculator divides fixed costs by the contribution per unit to find how many units you need to sell. Selling beyond that point generates profit, while selling below it leaves a loss.
What if my price is lower than my variable cost?::Then contribution per unit is negative and every sale makes your position worse. There is no break-even point at that price. The tool shows a clear message asking you to raise the price above variable cost, and it does not report a misleading unit count.
Why do you round break-even units up?::Because units are whole items. If the exact answer is 200.3 units, selling 200 leaves a small part of fixed costs uncovered, so you need 201 sales. The tool shows both the exact decimal and the rounded whole number so you can see the difference.
How is break-even revenue calculated?::It is the whole unit count multiplied by the price per unit, which is the sales value needed at that volume. You can also reach it by dividing fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio. Both routes agree once the unit count is rounded.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Every figure is computed locally in your browser from the numbers you enter, with no upload and no account. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How do you read a break-even result?
page.guidance:
The break-even point is where total revenue equals total costs, leaving zero profit. The Break-Even Point Calculator divides fixed costs by contribution per unit, that is price per unit minus variable cost per unit, and rounds up to a whole unit because you cannot sell part of one. Read the result as the volume you must reach in the same period as your fixed costs: monthly costs give a monthly target. Multiply the whole unit count by price for break-even revenue, or divide fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio when you track sales in currency.

For a monthly product with 4,000 currency units of fixed costs, a price of 50 and a variable cost of 30 per unit, each sale contributes 20, so the target is 200 units and 10,000 in revenue. Use that figure as a go or no-go line: compare your realistic monthly demand with 200 units before committing to the launch, and if demand falls short, raise the price or cut the variable cost to lower the threshold.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Rent vs. Buy Quick Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A rent versus buy calculator compares what you spend as a tenant with what you spend as an owner over the same number of years. This tool takes five inputs: monthly rent, home price, down payment, annual mortgage rate and holding period in whole years. It returns the rent paid over the period, the net cost of buying and selling at the end, the difference, and the first year where buying becomes cheaper.

For renting, the tool starts with your monthly rent and raises it by three percent each year, then adds twelve payments for every year in the holding period. For buying, it splits the price into a loan and a down payment, works out the level monthly principal and interest payment on a thirty year term, and tracks the loan balance year by year. Property tax at one percent, insurance at 0.35 percent and maintenance at one percent of the purchase price are added every year. Closing costs of two percent of the price are paid up front, and selling costs of six percent of the value are subtracted at exit. The home value grows by three percent a year.

The net buying cost is the down payment, closing costs, all monthly payments and all yearly carrying costs, minus the equity left after selling. Comparing that figure with cumulative rent gives the difference shown in the result. A break-even year appears when the net buying cost first falls below cumulative rent. These are fixed assumptions, not a forecast: local taxes, insurance, rent growth and price changes vary widely. Every calculation runs in your browser.
page.features:
Five inputs::Monthly rent, home price, down payment, interest rate and holding years are the only values you need.
Stated assumptions::Tax, insurance, maintenance, closing, selling, appreciation and rent growth are fixed and shown in the tool.
Level mortgage payment::Principal and interest use a thirty year fixed term, with the balance recalculated every year.
Net of sale::Buying cost subtracts the equity left after a six percent selling cost at the end of the period.
Break-even year::The result marks the first year when the net cost of buying falls below cumulative rent.
page.exampleInput:
Monthly rent: 2000
Home price: 300000
Down payment: 60000
Interest rate: 5 percent
Holding period: 10 years
page.exampleOutput:
Total rent paid: 275133
Net cost to buy: 107341
Buying cheaper by: 167792
Monthly principal and interest: 1288.37
Break-even year: 2
page.exampleNote: Rent and home value both grow three percent a year under the fixed assumptions, so buying pulls ahead from year two.
page.mistakes:
Comparing only monthly payments::A mortgage payment hides interest, tax, insurance and maintenance, so compare total cash cost instead.
Ignoring the sale::Equity is not spendable until you sell. The tool subtracts selling costs and shows the net figure.
Forgetting rent growth::Rent rarely stays flat. This tool raises it three percent a year, which changes the comparison over a long hold.
Treating assumptions as facts::Local tax rates, insurance and price growth differ, so read the result as a what-if rather than a forecast.
page.limits:
Holding period runs from 1 to 40 whole years.
Interest rate is limited to 0 to 25 percent.
Down payment must be below the home price.
Figures use decimal currency units and are rounded for display.
page.faqs:
What does the rent versus buy comparison actually measure?::It measures the net cash cost of each path over the same holding period. Rent is the sum of twelve monthly payments per year with a three percent annual increase. Buying is the down payment, closing costs, monthly mortgage payments and yearly carrying costs, minus the equity you keep after selling. The lower net cost wins.
How is the break-even year found?::The tool builds a row for every year in your holding period. Each row compares rent paid so far with the net cost of buying and selling at that point. The break-even year is the first row where the buying cost drops below the rent total. If that never happens, the result says buying has not broken even.
Which assumptions does the calculator use?::It uses a thirty year fixed mortgage, one percent property tax, 0.35 percent insurance and one percent maintenance on the purchase price each year. Closing costs are two percent up front, selling costs are six percent of value, and both rent and home value grow three percent a year. All are shown in the tool.
Can I use this for a real purchase decision?::Use it as a quick screen, not a full analysis. It skips income tax effects, loan points, extra payments, renovation costs and local rent controls. A real decision also depends on how long you will stay and what your local market does, so weigh those factors alongside the number.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. All five inputs and the full year by year schedule are computed locally in your browser, with no upload and no account. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: When does buying beat renting over time?
page.guidance:
The Rent versus Buy Calculator compares the cash you pay renting with the net cost of buying and selling over your chosen holding period. It reports total rent paid, net cost to buy, the difference, and the first year when buying turns cheaper. Read net cost to buy as down payment, closing costs, mortgage payments and yearly carrying costs minus the equity left after a six percent selling cost. The yearly table shows that net figure if you sold at each year end, so the break-even year is where buying first undercuts cumulative rent.

If you plan to stay three years, compare that span with the break-even year: with 2,000 currency units of monthly rent, a 300,000 home, 60,000 down and a 5 percent rate, buying turns cheaper in year two under the tool's assumptions, so a three-year stay favors buying. At one year renting wins, because closing and selling costs have not been recovered. Match the break-even year to your real planned stay before acting on the figure.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Video & File Size Estimator?
page.whatIs:
A video file size estimator converts a bitrate or a data rate and a duration into an approximate number of megabytes. This tool offers two ways in. Bitrate mode takes megabits per second and a duration in minutes; a resolution shortcut fills a typical bitrate for 480p, 720p, 1080p, 1440p or 4K. Data-rate mode takes megabytes per minute instead, which is useful when you know how much storage a camera or editor writes.

The arithmetic is simple. In bitrate mode, size in megabytes equals bitrate multiplied by duration in seconds, divided by eight, because eight megabits make one megabyte. In data-rate mode, size equals megabytes per minute multiplied by minutes. A two percent allowance is then added for the container header and indexing that sit around the media stream. The tool reports the result in decimal megabytes and gigabytes, using one thousand megabytes per gigabyte, then shows how many such files fit on 1 GB, 64 GB, 256 GB and 1 TB of storage.

Real files rarely match the estimate exactly. Variable bitrate encoding shifts data toward complex scenes and away from simple ones, audio tracks add their own stream, and different containers add different overhead. Two percent is a middle estimate, not a measured value. Use the figure to plan storage, compare recording settings or choose an upload target, and check the real file size after export. Every calculation happens in your browser and nothing you enter is uploaded.

Two input modes::Use bitrate in megabits per second or a data rate in megabytes per minute, whichever number you know.
Resolution shortcuts::480p, 720p, 1080p, 1440p and 4K fill typical streaming bitrates you can then edit.
Duration in minutes::Enter any run time from a short clip up to one week, then see the size update instantly.
Storage counts::See how many finished files fit on 1 GB, 64 GB, 256 GB and 1 TB devices.
Plain assumptions::Decimal gigabytes and a two percent container allowance are stated in the result.

page.mistakes:
Mixing bits and bytes::Bitrate is measured in megabits per second while file size is measured in megabytes, so divide by eight.
Using binary gigabytes::The tool uses one thousand megabytes per gigabyte, matching drive labels rather than operating system alerts.
Ignoring audio::The estimate covers the video stream and container allowance, not a separate high quality audio track.
Expecting exact sizes::Variable bitrate encoding and scene complexity move real files above or below the estimate.
page.limits:
Duration accepts values from 1 to 10080 minutes.
Bitrate is capped at 1000 megabits per second.

page.faqs:
How do I estimate a video file size from a bitrate?::Multiply the bitrate in megabits per second by the run time in seconds, then divide by eight to get megabytes. The tool does that for you and adds a two percent container allowance. A 10 megabit per second stream running for two hours produces about 9180 megabytes, or 9.18 gigabytes.
What is the difference between a bitrate and a data rate?::A bitrate counts megabits per second, which is how encoders and streaming services describe quality. A data rate counts megabytes per minute, which is closer to what a camera writes to storage. The tool accepts both and shows the megabits per second equivalent of a data rate in the result.
Why is the real file different from the estimate?::Most video uses variable bitrate encoding, so complex scenes consume more data and simple scenes consume less. Audio tracks, subtitles and metadata also add bytes, and containers differ in overhead. The two percent allowance is a reasonable middle estimate for planning, but only an export tells you the exact size.
Which storage units does the calculator use?::It uses decimal units, so one gigabyte is one thousand megabytes and one terabyte is one thousand gigabytes. That matches the capacity printed on drives and memory cards. Operating systems often report binary units, which makes the same file look slightly larger in a properties dialog.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika team. Bitrate, duration and data rate math runs entirely in your browser with no upload, no account and no stored files. Reviewed 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: How do you estimate a video's file size?
page.guidance:
A video file size estimate is the bitrate in megabits per second times the run time in seconds, divided by eight, plus a two percent container allowance. The Video & File Size Estimator runs that calculation and also takes a data rate in megabytes per minute when that is the number you have. It reports decimal megabytes and gigabytes, with 1,000 megabytes per gigabyte, then shows how many finished files fit on 1 GB, 64 GB, 256 GB and 1 TB devices. Treat the headline figure as a planning estimate and confirm the exact size after export.

For a two-hour recording at 10 megabits per second, the estimate is about 9,180 megabytes, or 9.18 GB, so a 64 GB card holds roughly seven files. Use that count to plan a shoot: divide the card's labelled capacity by the estimated size, then leave headroom for audio and variable bitrate, which push real exports above the estimate. If you need a set number of files per card, lower the bitrate until the fit count reaches your target.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Date Difference Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A date difference calculator measures the distance between two calendar dates and expresses it in the unit you choose. Our tool accepts a start date and a target date, then reports the span as total days, whole weeks with leftover days, whole calendar months with leftover days, or a full countdown broken into years, months, weeks and days. A third date, set to today by default, adds a second reference gap so you can compare the target against the present as well.

The day count is pure arithmetic: convert each date to a UTC day number and subtract, so daylight saving transitions never add or remove an hour. Inclusive mode adds one day to cover both endpoints; exclusive mode leaves the plain gap. Weeks are the whole sevens in that day count, and the remainder is the leftover days. Calendar months are counted by stepping the start date forward one month at a time until the next step would pass the target. When a month is shorter, the day clamps to its last valid date, so 31 January plus one month lands on 28 or 29 February.

The full countdown walks the same span in stages. It adds whole years first, then whole months from that anniversary, then whole weeks, then the remaining days. The breakdown strip shows that chain from start to target, and the comparison figure is the gap between the other date and the target under the same inclusive or exclusive rule.

Time of day is ignored because the inputs are dates, not timestamps. Leap days are handled by the calendar, so a span crossing 29 February counts them correctly. Results are rounded down to whole units, and a target earlier than the start is rejected with a prompt to swap the dates rather than showing a negative countdown.

Start: 2026-01-15
Target: 2026-11-27
Another date: 2026-06-01
Mode: Days
Counting: exclusive
page.exampleOutput:
Total days: 316
Whole weeks: 45 weeks and 1 day
Calendar months: 10 months and 12 days
Whole years: 0 years
From another date: 179 days

Enter the target date, the final day you want to count to.

page.mistakes:
Counting the gap as inclusive::Both endpoints add one day to the total, so a Friday to Monday span is four days inclusive and three exclusive.
Mixing clock times into a date span::The inputs are calendar dates, so a late night start and an early morning target on the next day count as one day apart.
Assuming every month is 30 days::Calendar months vary from 28 to 31 days, and a short month clamps the day when stepping forward.
Ignoring the comparison date::The another date field starts at today, so changing it updates only the comparison figure, not the main span.
page.limits:
The target date must fall on or after the start date.
Only years from 1000 to 9999 can be entered in a date field.
Only whole calendar units are shown, with no hours or minutes.
page.faqs:
What does inclusive counting change?::Exclusive counting measures the plain gap between two dates, so the same day on two consecutive dates is one day. Inclusive counting adds the final day, so that pair becomes two days. The option affects day totals, leftover days and the comparison figure, while whole years and months stay anchored to calendar boundaries.
How are calendar months calculated?::The tool steps the start date forward one month at a time until the next step would pass the target. If the target month is shorter, the day clamps to its last valid date, so 31 January plus one month lands on 28 or 29 February. The leftover days are then counted from that clamped date.
Why is there an another date field?::The another date field defaults to today and gives you a second reference point for the same target. It is useful when you want a countdown from today while also comparing two historical dates. Changing it updates the comparison figure only and never changes the main span between start and target.
Does daylight saving affect the result?::No. Each date is read as a UTC calendar day, so a daylight saving change cannot add or remove an hour from the span. Leap days are counted normally by the calendar. Time of day is ignored, which keeps results stable across browsers and time zones.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika time desk. Every calculation runs in your browser, and only your mode and counting choice are remembered. Last updated 27 November 2026.
page.guidanceTitle: What does the date difference result show?
page.guidance:
The Date Difference & Countdown Calculator measures the span between a start date and a target date in days, weeks with leftover days, calendar months, or a full countdown of years, months, weeks and days. Dates are read as UTC calendar days, so daylight saving cannot change the gap. Exclusive counting gives the plain distance, inclusive counting adds the final day. A third date, defaulting to today, supplies a separate comparison figure that updates on its own. Choose days for exact scheduling and full countdown for a readable long-term breakdown.

From 15 January 2026 to 27 November 2026 the tool returns 316 days exclusive, or 317 inclusive, which matters when a contract counts both end dates. To track a deadline from today, leave the third date on its default and read the comparison figure, then change it to an earlier milestone to see how the gap shifts. Months follow calendar boundaries and clamp in short months, so 31 January plus one month lands on 28 or 29 February.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an Age Calculator?
page.whatIs:
An age calculator measures the time between a birth date and a reference date and reports it as whole years, months and days. The same span is converted into total days, whole weeks and calendar months, and the tool also finds the next birthday with its weekday. Enter a birth date and an as of date to get the full breakdown.

Age is not a simple subtraction. The calculator first steps forward in whole years until the next birthday would pass the reference date, then steps forward in whole months from that anniversary, then counts the remaining days. When a birthday falls on 29 February, the anniversary in a non leap year is clamped to 28 February. Day totals use UTC calendar days, so daylight saving changes cannot add or remove an hour.

The as of date starts at today and can be changed to any later date. That makes the tool useful for historical questions, such as how old someone was on a wedding date, and for future planning, such as the age at a graduation. The next birthday countdown reports both the number of days remaining and the weekday on which that birthday falls. The weekday of birth is calculated from the same calendar date.

For a second way to check a span between any two calendar dates, see the reference at https://www.timeanddate.com/date/duration.html. This tool performs every step locally in your browser and never sends a birth date to a server.
page.howToTitle: How to calculate your age

page.guidanceTitle: How does the age calculation work?
page.guidance:
The exact age card is the main answer. It shows whole years, then the months and days completed after the last birthday. Total days is a straight count between the two dates, while whole weeks and calendar months describe the same span in different units. The next birthday row shows a date, the days remaining and the weekday, so you can plan ahead without doing a second calculation. A result of zero days means the birthday falls on the as of date itself.

For a person born on 15 June 1990 and an as of date of 27 November 2026, the tool reports 36 years, 5 months and 12 days, or 13,314 days in total. That is 1,902 whole weeks with no leftover days. If you need the age on 1 January 2020 instead, change only the as of date and the exact age becomes 29 years, 6 months and 17 days. The birth date and all other rows update automatically.

Birth date: 15 June 1990
As of date: 27 November 2026
page.exampleOutput:
36 years, 5 months, 12 days
13,314 total days
1,902 weeks + 0 days
437 calendar months + 12 days
Born on a Friday
Next birthday: 15 June 2027 (200 days, Tuesday)

page.features:
Exact age::Years, months and days are calculated with real calendar boundaries and month end clamping.
Day totals::Total days, whole weeks with leftovers and calendar months all come from one UTC day count.
Birthday countdown::Days to the next birthday and its weekday are shown with the exact date.
Flexible reference::The as of date starts at today and can move to any past or future day.
Plain text copy::A formatted summary is ready for the clipboard with the Copy action.

page.useCases:

Age milestone tracking::Check when a future age milestone arrives by moving the as of date forward.
Days lived comparison::Compare total days, weeks and months to understand a long life span in different units.
page.faqs:
How is exact age calculated?::The tool moves forward in whole years from the birth date until the next birthday would pass the as of date. It then adds whole months from that anniversary and finishes with the remaining days. Month ends are clamped, so a 31 January birth clamps to the last day of shorter months, and a leap day birth uses 28 February in non leap years.
Why can I change the as of date?::The as of date lets you ask about any point in time, not just today. Historical questions include the age on a wedding day or a past application date. Future questions include the age at graduation or a retirement milestone. The field starts on today and the Today action restores it in one click.
What is the difference between total days and calendar months?::Total days is a straight count of UTC calendar days between the two dates. Calendar months advance by real month boundaries, which range from 28 to 31 days, and clamp when the target month is shorter. Both numbers describe the same span, but total days is exact while calendar months follow the calendar.
How does the next birthday countdown work?::The tool finds the first birthday on or after the as of date and counts the days to it. If the as of date is the birthday itself the countdown is zero. For a 29 February birth date, the anniversary in a common year is treated as 28 February, which keeps the countdown continuous.
Does daylight saving change the result?::No. Each date is read as a UTC calendar day, so a clock change cannot add or remove an hour. Leap days are counted normally by the calendar. Time of day is not part of the input, which keeps results stable across browsers, devices and time zones.
Is my birth date stored or uploaded?::No. The calculation happens entirely in your browser. The tool keeps no birth dates in local storage and makes no network request with your input. Only the plain text summary is created on demand so you can copy it yourself.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Sales Tax Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A sales tax and VAT calculator works out either the tax added to a net price or the tax already included in a gross price. In add tax mode it takes a net amount and a percentage, then returns the tax and the gross total. In extract tax mode it reverses the same relationship and reports the base net amount and the embedded tax.

The addition formula is tax equals net amount multiplied by the rate divided by one hundred. The gross total is the net amount plus that tax. Extraction divides the gross amount by one plus the rate as a decimal, which gives the net base. The embedded tax is the gross amount minus that base. Using division rather than multiplying by the rate avoids a small overstatement that is common when people try to reverse a percentage.

Quick rate pills cover the common zero, five, ten and twenty percent cases, and a custom field accepts any other rate. An optional quantity divides the total into per unit net, tax and gross figures. A searchable currency picker covers a wide list of ISO codes and formats every money value with the chosen currency.

Tax rules differ by country and locality. The authoritative guidance for United States sellers is at https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/sales-tax. This tool does the arithmetic only, in your browser, and never sends an amount to a server.
page.howToTitle: How to calculate sales tax
page.howTo:
Choose Add Tax or Extract Tax to match the price you already have.
Enter the net amount for add mode or the gross amount for extract mode.
Pick a quick rate pill, or choose Custom and type an exact percentage.
Set a quantity when you want per unit net, tax and total figures.
Search and select a currency from the full ISO code list.
Read the large total card and the tax and net cards on the right.
Copy the breakdown for your records with the Copy action.
page.guidanceTitle: How does sales tax extraction work?
page.guidance:
Read the large total card as the final answer. In add tax mode that card is the gross price a customer pays, and the tax card shows how much of it is tax. In extract tax mode the large card is the gross price you entered, while the base net card is the amount left after removing tax. The rate card repeats the percentage in use, and the per unit rows split every figure by the quantity you entered.

A net price of 120.00 with a 20 percent rate adds 24.00 in tax and gives a gross total of 144.00. With four units, the per unit figures are 30.00 net, 6.00 tax and 36.00 gross. Reversing the same example, a gross price of 144.00 at 20 percent gives a net base of 120.00 and embedded tax of 24.00. Multiplying 144.00 by 20 percent would wrongly give 28.80, which is why extraction uses division by 1.20.
page.exampleInput:
Mode: Add Tax
Amount: 120.00
Rate: 20%
Quantity: 3
Currency: USD
page.exampleOutput:
Tax: 24.00 USD
Total: 144.00 USD
Per unit: 40.00 net + 8.00 tax = 48.00 total
page.exampleNote: Switching to Extract Tax with 144.00 as the amount returns the same 24.00 tax and 120.00 net.
page.features:
Two calculation modes::Add tax to a net price or extract tax from a gross price with the same rate.
Quick and custom rates::Common percentages are one click away, with a precise custom field for everything else.
Per unit breakdown::An optional quantity splits net, tax and total across identical items.
Searchable currencies::A broad ISO list formats every money value in the currency you choose.
Inline fix hints::Missing or invalid amounts, rates and quantities show a short correction message.
Copyable breakdown::A plain text summary keeps inputs and results together for records.
page.useCasesTitle: When to use Sales Tax Calculator
page.useCases:
Retail price checks::Confirm the shelf price after adding the local rate to a net cost.
Invoice reconciliation::Recover the net base and embedded tax from a paid gross invoice.
Marketplace comparisons::Compare per unit prices when a cart contains several identical items.
Travel budgeting::Switch currency codes while checking how much tax is included in a receipt.
page.faqs:
What is the difference between add tax and extract tax?::Add tax starts with a net price and adds a percentage to reach the gross price. Extract tax starts with a gross price and removes the embedded percentage to recover the net price. The two modes use inverse formulas, so choosing the wrong one changes the result even when the rate is identical.
How is tax extracted from a gross price?::The net base is the gross amount divided by one plus the rate expressed as a decimal. For a 20 percent rate the divisor is 1.20. The embedded tax is the gross amount minus that net base. This avoids the common error of multiplying the gross amount by the rate, which overstates the tax.
Can I use any tax rate?::Yes. The quick pills cover zero, five, ten and twenty percent for speed, and the Custom option accepts any other percentage with decimals. The calculator validates the rate and shows an inline fix hint if the value is missing or not a number.
Why does quantity appear in the result?::Quantity is optional and is used only to divide the net amount, tax and gross total into per unit figures. It is useful when a cart contains several identical items or when you want the tax contribution of one unit. Leaving it at one shows the whole order.
Which currencies are available?::The searchable picker covers a broad ISO 4217 list, including the US dollar, euro, British pound, Canadian dollar, Australian dollar, Indian rupee and many more. Type a code or part of a currency name to narrow the list, then select the one that matches your price.
Does this tool know my local tax rules?::No. It applies only the percentage you enter. Real sales tax and VAT rules depend on jurisdiction, product category and registration status, so check the relevant tax authority for the correct rate before relying on a figure.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Savings Goal Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A savings goal calculator estimates how long it will take to reach a target amount from a starting balance and a regular deposit. It also reports how much of the final balance comes from your own contributions and how much comes from interest or investment growth. Choose a daily, weekly or monthly habit before entering the amount.

The tool converts a daily or weekly habit into an equivalent monthly deposit, then simulates month by month. Growth is applied first using an effective monthly rate derived from the quoted annual rate and the chosen compounding frequency. The deposit is added at the end of each month, and the simulation stops as soon as the balance reaches the goal. Daily, monthly, quarterly and yearly compounding are supported.

The result shows the number of months, a years and months timeline, total contributed, growth and the ending balance. Quarter checkpoints show the balance at twenty five, fifty, seventy five and one hundred percent of the timeline. If the goal is unreachable within fifty years, the tool suggests a larger deposit instead of showing a misleading date.

For consumer guidance on building an emergency fund, see https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/saving/. Every projection here is calculated in your browser and no amount is uploaded.
page.howToTitle: How to use Savings Goal Calculator
page.howTo:
Choose whether you save every day, every week or every month.
Enter the amount you set aside at that frequency.
Type your target goal and any starting savings.
Add an annual return rate, or leave it at zero for a simple sum.
Pick the compounding frequency that matches the account.
Read the months to goal card and the contribution and growth cards.
Copy the plan with the Copy action to keep the assumptions together.
page.guidanceTitle: How compounding frequency changes your savings timeline
page.guidance:
The months to goal card is the headline answer, and the note beneath it converts that into years and months. Total contributed counts only the recurring deposits, while growth is the extra amount earned from the annual rate. The final balance is the sum of starting savings, contributions and growth. Checkpoint rows show the balance at four points along the timeline so you can see progress rather than only the finish line.

Saving 300 each month toward a 12,000 goal with 2,000 already saved and a five percent annual return reaches the target in about 29 months. Without any interest the same goal needs about 34 months. If you switch the habit to 10 each day, the tool converts that to about 304 each month and the timeline shortens. When the contribution is zero and the return is zero, the result explains that the goal cannot grow and asks for a deposit or a rate.
page.exampleInput:
Goal: 12,000
Starting savings: 2,000
Monthly contribution: 300
Annual return: 5%
Compounding: Monthly
page.exampleOutput:
Months to goal: 31 (2 years, 7 months)
Total contributed: 9,300
Interest growth: 880
Final balance: 12,180
page.exampleNote: The final month adds the last deposit and crosses the target, so the balance shown sits slightly above the goal. Growth is separated from money you contributed.
page.features:
Flexible saving cadence::Choose a daily, weekly or monthly habit and the tool converts it to a monthly figure.
Compound growth::Annual rate and compounding frequency combine into an effective monthly rate.
Contribution split::Total deposits and earned growth are reported separately from the starting balance.
Quarter checkpoints::Four progress markers show the balance at twenty five, fifty, seventy five and one hundred percent.
Actionable unreachable state::A shortfall and suggested deposit replace a misleading date.
Private planning::All projections run locally with no uploads of your amounts.
page.useCases:
Emergency fund planning::Estimate how long a monthly deposit takes to build a three month expense buffer.
Daily saving habit::Convert a small daily amount into a realistic timeline for a larger goal.
Vacation budgeting::See whether a target can be reached before a travel date with a chosen return rate.
Rate comparison::Change the annual rate to understand how compounding affects the finish date.
page.faqs:
What happens when I choose a daily or weekly habit?::The amount you enter is converted into an equivalent monthly deposit using 365 days per year or 52 weeks per year divided by 12. The projection still advances one month at a time, which keeps interest and deposits aligned. The result note always reports the original habit alongside the monthly figure.
How does compounding frequency change the result?::A higher quoted annual rate with more frequent compounding produces more growth because interest is added more often. The tool converts each frequency to an equivalent monthly growth rate, so daily, monthly, quarterly and yearly options remain comparable and the month by month simulation stays consistent.
What if I cannot save anything yet?::Enter zero as the amount and zero as the annual rate. The calculator then explains that the balance cannot change and suggests adding either a regular deposit or a positive return. It never invents a completion date for a goal that cannot be reached.
Why is there a fifty year limit?::The simulation is capped at 600 months so the result stays finite and predictable. If the goal is still out of reach at that point, the tool reports the shortfall and suggests the smallest monthly deposit that would reach the target inside the window.
Are the growth figures guaranteed?::No. The annual rate is an assumption you enter, not a promise. Actual returns vary, and fees, taxes and changes in contribution amount are not modelled. Treat the projection as a planning estimate and review it when your circumstances change.
Is my savings data private?::Yes. Every calculation runs in your browser. The tool stores only display options such as the chosen cadence, never your goal, balance or rate, and it makes no network request with those numbers.
page.trustBody: Built by the Toolpika money desk. The simulation applies growth before each month end deposit and caps at 600 months. Reviewed 27 November 2026. Consumer guidance is available at https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/saving/.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Fuel Cost Calculator?
page.whatIs:
A fuel cost and mileage calculator estimates how much fuel a trip needs and what that fuel costs. It accepts a one way or return distance, a fuel efficiency figure in km per liter, liters per 100 km, US MPG or UK MPG, and a price that follows the chosen unit. An optional split count divides the total between passengers.

All efficiency figures are converted to kilometers per liter internally. One mile is 1.609344 kilometers, one US gallon is 3.785411784 liters and one imperial gallon is 4.54609 liters. US MPG is multiplied by 0.425144 and UK MPG by 0.354006 to reach kilometers per liter. The price field is relabelled to per liter, per US gallon or per imperial gallon so the unit always matches the efficiency choice.

Round trip doubles the distance before any division, which doubles fuel and total cost while leaving cost per kilometer almost unchanged. The result reports liters needed, US gallons needed, total trip cost, cost per person and cost per kilometer. A plain text estimate can be copied for a shared journey.

For official fuel economy data and test procedures, see https://www.fueleconomy.gov/. This calculator uses only the numbers you enter and performs every conversion locally in your browser.
page.howToTitle: How to use Fuel Cost Calculator
page.howTo:
Choose kilometers or miles for the trip distance.
Enter the one way distance and turn on round trip if you are returning.
Set how many people will share the cost.
Choose the efficiency unit printed on the vehicle or listing.
Enter the efficiency value in that unit.
Type the fuel price in the unit shown beside the price field.
Read the total cost card and copy the estimate for your group.
page.guidanceTitle: How fuel price units change the estimate
page.guidance:
The large cost card is the total fuel spend for the whole trip. The liters figure shows the physical fuel needed, and the gallons figure is the same volume in US gallons for easy comparison with quoted figures. Cost per person divides the total by the split count, while cost per kilometer stays comparable between one way and return journeys because both cost and distance double together. The price hint always names the unit in use.

A 240 kilometer trip at 7.5 liters per 100 km needs 18 liters of fuel. At 1.85 per liter the trip costs 33.30, or 16.65 each for two people. Turning on round trip makes it 480 kilometers, 36 liters and 66.60 total, still about 0.14 per kilometer. If the car is quoted at 31.4 US MPG instead, the same 240 kilometers needs the same 18 liters because 31.4 MPG converts to about 13.35 kilometers per liter.
page.exampleInput:
Distance: 240 km
Efficiency: 7.5 L/100km
Price: 1.85 per liter
Round trip: off
Split: 2
page.exampleOutput:
Fuel needed: 18 liters (4.755 US gallons)
Trip fuel cost: 33.30
Cost per person: 16.65
Cost per kilometer: 0.14

page.whatIsTitle: What is Cooking Converter?
page.whatIs:
A cooking measurement converter translates kitchen volumes and weights such as cup, tablespoon, teaspoon, milliliter, fluid ounce, gram, kilogram and ounce. When a recipe crosses between volume and weight, the result depends on the ingredient, so this tool asks for a density from a short list that includes flour, sugar, rice, butter, oats and liquids.

Volume units are resolved through milliliters using one cup equals 240 ml, one tablespoon equals 15 ml, one teaspoon equals 5 ml and one US fluid ounce equals 30 ml. Weight units use grams, with 1000 grams per kilogram and about 28.35 grams per ounce. Volume to weight conversions multiply the cup count by the grams per cup of the chosen ingredient. Weight to volume divides by the same value.

The density list reflects typical kitchen measurements. All purpose flour is about 120 grams per cup, granulated sugar about 200, packed brown sugar about 220, uncooked white rice about 185, butter about 227 and rolled oats about 90. Liquids such as water, broth and milk use about 240 grams per cup. The reference row always shows the one unit relationship used for the chosen ingredient.

Baking is sensitive to how an ingredient is packed and measured. A reference chart from King Arthur Baking is at https://www.kingarthurbaking.com/learn/ingredient-weight-chart. This tool performs all conversions locally and keeps your amounts in the browser.
page.howToTitle: How to use Cooking Converter
page.howTo:

page.guidanceTitle: How Do Volume and Weight Conversions Work?
page.guidance:
The large amount card is the converted quantity in the target unit. The ingredient row names the density used, and the reference row shows the one unit relationship, such as one cup of flour equal to 120 grams. Volume to volume and weight to weight conversions do not need density, so changing the ingredient leaves those results unchanged. Only volume to weight and weight to volume depend on how tightly the ingredient packs.

One cup of all purpose flour converts to about 120 grams, while one cup of water converts to about 240 grams. That difference is why a generic cup to gram chart can ruin a cake. For a recipe calling for 225 grams of flour, the tool gives about 1.875 cups, which is close to one and seven eighths cups. Switching to butter gives about 0.99 cups for the same weight because butter is much denser than flour.

To: g
Ingredient: All-Purpose Flour

Density: 120 g per cup

page.faqs:
Why does the ingredient matter?::A cup is a measure of volume, while a gram is a measure of weight. Flour, sugar, rice and butter pack differently, so the same cup holds very different weights. The ingredient selector supplies grams per cup, which makes volume to weight and weight to volume results realistic for baking and cooking.
Which volume units are supported?::The tool supports cup, tablespoon, teaspoon, milliliter and US fluid ounce. One cup is 240 ml, one tablespoon is 15 ml, one teaspoon is 5 ml and one fluid ounce is 30 ml. Changing between these units is pure volume arithmetic and does not need a density.
How accurate is a cup to gram result?::It is a practical kitchen estimate based on typical grams per cup values. How you spoon, level or pack an ingredient changes the real weight. A digital scale is more accurate, especially for baking. Use the reference row to understand the assumption behind the result.
What does the swap control do?::Swap exchanges the from and to units without changing the amount or ingredient. It is useful when you have a weight in grams and want cups, or when you want to check the reverse conversion. The hero value and reference row update immediately.
Can I convert kilograms or ounces?::Yes. Kilograms and ounces are included alongside grams. One kilogram is 1000 grams and one ounce is about 28.35 grams. Weight to weight conversions are exact unit changes, while weight to volume conversions still use the selected ingredient density.
Does the tool store my recipe amounts?::No. Every conversion runs in your browser and no amount is sent to a server. The tool keeps no recipe history, and the Copy action simply places the formatted conversion on your clipboard.

page.whatIsTitle: What is Stopwatch Timer?
page.whatIs:
A stopwatch and lap timer measures elapsed time with high precision and records split points without resetting the clock. This browser tool uses performance.now for timing, so the display keeps running accurately even when the page is busy. It supports start, pause, lap and reset, along with keyboard shortcuts for the two most common actions.

Each lap stores two values. The lap duration is the time since the previous lap, and the split is the total time since the start. The lap list highlights the fastest and slowest durations so you can spot pacing patterns at a glance. Animations are disabled from the timing path, and requestAnimationFrame only updates the display.

Press Space while the workspace is focused to start or pause, and press L while running to record a lap. The shortcut handler ignores text fields and buttons, so typing in other parts of the page never changes the timer. The Copy and Export actions turn the lap list into plain text with the elapsed time, lap durations and splits.

Stopwatches measure elapsed time rather than wall clock time, which makes them suitable for sports, study sessions and process timing. A short background is at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stopwatch. Everything here runs locally and the lap data is never uploaded.

page.howTo:

page.guidanceTitle: How Do Laps and Splits Work?
page.guidance:
The elapsed display is the time since the timer started, including every lap. The lap table separates lap duration from split time, so a slow lap is easy to spot even when the running total looks steady. The fastest and slowest rows are highlighted with calm accent colours. Laps are only recorded while the timer is running, and a lap with no elapsed time is ignored rather than stored.

A sample session with splits at 12.34, 22.21 and 37.23 seconds produces three laps of 12.34, 9.87 and 15.02 seconds. The second lap is the fastest and the third is the slowest, while the final split equals the elapsed display. This makes the table useful for interval training: repeat the same distance and compare lap durations, then copy the list to track progress over several sessions.

Lap 1: 00:12.34, split 00:12.34
Lap 2: 00:09.87, split 00:22.21
Lap 3: 00:15.02, split 00:37.23
Fastest: lap 2, slowest: lap 3
page.exampleNote: Lap duration resets at each lap, while the split keeps counting from the start.
page.features:
High precision clock::performance.now drives elapsed time and the display shows hundredths of a second.
Lap and split rows::Every lap shows its own duration and the total time from the start.
Fastest and slowest::Pacing extremes are highlighted without extra controls.

page.useCases:
Interval training::Compare lap durations across repeated runs to see where pace drops.
Study sessions::Time focused blocks and keep splits for a study log.
Process timing::Measure how long a repeatable task takes across several attempts.

page.faqs:
How precise is the timer?::The clock uses performance.now, a high resolution browser timer measured in milliseconds, and the display shows hundredths of a second. The display is refreshed with requestAnimationFrame while the underlying value is read from the monotonic clock, so rendering delays do not change the recorded time.
What is the difference between a lap and a split?::A lap is the time since the previous lap. A split is the total time since the start. The table shows both values for every row, which lets you compare individual effort with the overall pace without doing subtraction yourself.
Which keyboard shortcuts are supported?::Space starts or pauses the timer when focus is not in a text field or button. L records a lap while the timer is running. The handler ignores repeated key events and modified shortcuts, so holding a key does not create duplicate laps.
Can I pause and resume without losing laps?::Yes. Pause holds the current elapsed time and the lap list stays intact. Starting again continues from the held time because the tool keeps the base duration and adds the new running interval. Reset clears both the clock and the laps.
Does the timer keep time in the background?::The elapsed value comes from the monotonic clock, so it stays correct when the tab is slow. The visual display only refreshes while animation frames are available. Pausing records the current value, so a hidden tab does not silently change a paused session.
Are my laps uploaded anywhere?::No. The timer, lap list and export all run in your browser. Nothing is stored in local storage and no network request is made with your session data. The export is created locally in your browser.

page.whatIsTitle: What is an electricity bill calculator?
page.whatIs:
An electricity bill estimator turns appliance wattage, daily hours and a price per kilowatt hour into a daily, monthly and yearly cost. It supports a watt or kilowatt switch, a month length from 1 to 31 days and a searchable currency picker. Several appliances can be added one at a time and the results update as a combined total.

The core formula is kilowatt hours equals watts multiplied by hours, divided by one thousand. A 2000 watt heater running four hours uses 8 kWh per day. Monthly usage is the daily figure multiplied by the shared month length, and yearly usage multiplies the monthly figure by twelve. Cost is usage multiplied by the price per kWh.

Each appliance can override the shared month length, which is useful for devices that run only on weekdays or during a shorter season. The breakdown lists the monthly kWh and cost of every appliance, and the large result card shows the combined monthly spend. The currency picker covers a broad ISO 4217 list and formats every money value consistently.

Actual bills also include fixed charges, tiered rates and taxes that this estimate does not model. General energy saving guidance is at https://www.energy.gov/energysaver. The estimator runs entirely in your browser and uploads no appliance data.

page.guidanceTitle: How to read your electricity estimate
page.guidance:
The large card is the combined monthly electricity cost across every appliance you added. The kWh cards show daily, monthly and yearly consumption before price, which makes it easy to see whether a high bill comes from heavy use or a high rate. The breakdown lists each appliance with its monthly kWh and cost, so the biggest contributor is obvious. Cost per appliance uses the same price per kWh as the total.

A 2000 watt heater used four hours a day consumes 8 kWh daily, or 240 kWh in a 30 day month. At 0.25 per kWh that is 60.00 per month. Add a 100 watt laptop for six hours, which uses 0.6 kWh per day and 18 kWh per month, and the combined monthly cost becomes 64.50. Over a year the two devices cost about 773.00 at the same rate.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a due date calculator?
page.whatIs:
A due date calculator estimates a pregnancy due date from a reference date. This tool supports three starting points: a last menstrual period, a conception date or an IVF transfer date. It applies the standard 280 day count from the last period, a 266 day offset from conception, or a transfer based offset that accounts for embryo age.

For a last menstrual period the due date is 280 days later. For conception the due date is 266 days later, because conception usually happens about two weeks after the period began. For IVF the tool subtracts fourteen days and the transfer day count from 280, then adds the remainder to the transfer date. A five day transfer therefore uses 261 days.

The result also reports the current gestational week and day measured from the last period equivalent, a trimester badge and four milestone dates. Those milestones cover the end of the first trimester at 13 weeks and 6 days, the midpoint at 20 weeks, the start of full term at 37 weeks and the end of the term window at 42 weeks.

This is a general calendar estimate and not medical advice. Dating can differ after an ultrasound. Clinical guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists is at https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/your-pregnancy-due-date. All calculations run locally in your browser.

page.howTo:

page.guidanceTitle: How to read your due date estimate
page.guidance:
The large card is the estimated due date. The gestational row counts weeks and days from the last period equivalent, which keeps all three methods comparable. The trimester badge is a simple calendar label, and the milestone rows show when the first trimester ends, the halfway point arrives and the full term window begins and ends. Days until the due date is measured from the as of date, not from today if you changed it.

A last menstrual period of 1 January 2026 gives an estimated due date of 8 October 2026. On 27 November 2026 the as of date is after that date, so the tool reports the weeks completed and marks the result as after the due date. If you know a conception date of 15 January instead, the due date moves to 22 October 2026. A five day IVF transfer on 15 January gives an offset of 261 days and a due date in early October.

Full term window: 17 September 2026 to 22 October 2026
page.exampleNote: Switch the method to conception with the same date and the due date moves to 24 September 2026.
page.features:
Three calculation methods::Last menstrual period, conception date and IVF transfer date all use the correct offset.
Day month year entry::Reference and as of dates use clear selects in reading order.
Gestational age::Weeks and days are measured from the last period equivalent.
Trimester badge::A simple calendar label shows the current trimester.
Milestone dates::First trimester end, midpoint and term window are listed with real dates.
Private estimate::All date arithmetic runs locally with no uploads.
page.useCases:
Early pregnancy planning::Turn a known period date into a calendar estimate for planning.
IVF dating::Translate a transfer date and embryo age into the standard due date convention.
Milestone preparation::See when the twenty week midpoint and full term window fall.
Record comparison::Change the as of date to check the gestational week on a past date.
page.faqs:
Which reference date should I use?::Use the date you know most reliably. A last menstrual period is the standard starting point and uses 280 days. Conception adds 266 days from the known date, and an IVF transfer uses 280 days minus fourteen days and minus the embryo age at transfer. Changing the method relabels the reference field.
How does the IVF offset work?::Pregnancy dating starts at the last period equivalent, which is about fourteen days before conception. For IVF the tool takes 280 days, subtracts fourteen days and subtracts the transfer day count. A three day transfer uses 263 days and a five day transfer uses 261 days from the transfer date.
What is gestational age measured from?::Gestational age is counted from the last period equivalent, even when you entered a conception or transfer date. This is the usual clinical convention and keeps results comparable across methods. The result shows whole weeks and remaining days as of the reference date you chose.
What do the milestone dates mean?::The end of the first trimester is 13 weeks and 6 days, the midpoint is 20 weeks, and the full term window runs from 37 weeks to 42 weeks from the last period equivalent. These are calendar markers from the same dating convention, not predictions of any specific event.
Is this medical advice?::No. This is a general calendar estimate based on the dates you enter. Ovulation timing, cycle length and ultrasound measurements can change the clinical date. Always discuss dating questions and any pregnancy concerns with a qualified healthcare professional.
Is my date information private?::Yes. The calculation runs entirely in your browser and no date is uploaded. Only the method and transfer day choice are remembered for convenience, never the reference date itself. Keep the reference date private on this device.

page.whatIsTitle: What is a Text Repeater?
page.whatIs:
A text repeater duplicates a word, phrase, sentence or emoji a chosen number of times and joins the copies with a separator. This tool accepts a repeat count from 1 to 500, offers quick chips for common counts and supports a new line, a space, a comma and space, or a custom delimiter.

An optional numbering switch prefixes each copy with its position, which is useful for lists, test data and numbered examples. Live counters show characters and lines in the input and in the output, so you can check the size of the result before copying it. The output can be copied or downloaded as a plain text file.

The separator controls exactly how copies are joined. A new line creates one copy per line, while a space keeps everything on one line. A custom delimiter accepts any string, such as a pipe, a tab-like mark or a short word. An empty custom delimiter is rejected with an inline fix hint because it would merge the copies together.

String repetition is a common programming operation, described in the JavaScript reference at https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/repeat. This tool performs the whole operation locally and never sends your text to a server.
page.howToTitle: How to use Text Repeater
page.howTo:
Type or paste the text, phrase or emoji you want to repeat.
Choose a quick count chip, or enter a count from 1 to 500.
Pick the separator that matches how you will use the output.
Type a custom delimiter only when you selected Custom.
Turn on line numbering if each copy should show its position.
Read the output character and line counters on the right.
Copy the output or download it as a text file.
page.guidanceTitle: How to choose the right separator
page.guidance:
The large count card shows how many copies are in the output, and the note beneath it gives the total output characters. Four counters describe the input and output separately, which makes it easy to predict the size of a block before you copy it. The preview shows the exact text that will be placed on your clipboard, including the separator and any numbering.

Five copies of a 12 character phrase with a new line separator produce about 75 characters including line breaks. The same five copies with a comma and space separator produce about 70 characters on one line. Turning on numbering adds the position and a dot to each line, which is convenient for numbered exercises but changes the character count. A custom delimiter such as three dashes is useful when importing a list into a spreadsheet.
page.exampleInput:
Text: Hello
Count: 3
Separator: New line
Numbering: on
page.exampleOutput:
1. Hello
2. Hello
3. Hello
Output characters: 26
Output lines: 3
page.exampleNote: Each numbered copy is eight characters, and two new lines bring the total to twenty-six characters across three lines.
page.features:
Counts to 500::Quick chips and a validated stepper cover common and custom repeat counts.
Four separators::New line, space, comma and space, or a custom delimiter of your choice.
Optional numbering::Prefix each copy with its position for lists and exercises.
Live counters::Input and output characters and lines update as you type.
Copy and download::Plain text output can be copied or saved as a file.
Private by design::All repetition runs locally with no uploads of your text.
page.useCases:
Test data generation::Create repeated rows for a spreadsheet or a form field.
Classroom exercises::Numbered lines give students a ready made practice sheet.
Copy preparation::Build a long repeated block without pressing paste hundreds of times.
Messaging drafts::Repeat a phrase or emoji with a clean separator for later editing.
page.faqs:
What is the maximum repeat count?::The count ranges from 1 to 500. Quick chips set 5, 10, 25, 50 or 100 in one click, and the stepper handles any other value in the range. A count outside the range shows a short fix hint rather than producing a huge block of text.
Which separators are available?::You can join copies with a new line, a single space, a comma followed by a space, or a custom delimiter of your choice. The custom field appears only when you select the custom option, and it must contain at least one character.
Does numbering change the text?::Yes. Numbering adds the position and a dot before each copy, so line one begins with one dot and a space. It does not change the text you entered. Turn it off when you need the clean phrase repeated without prefixes.
Why do I see four counters?::Input characters and lines describe what you typed. Output characters and lines describe the generated text. Comparing them helps you understand how the separator, count and numbering affect the final size before you copy or download it.
Can I repeat emoji?::Yes. The tool treats your input as text, so emoji, symbols and mixed scripts are all repeated exactly as entered. The character counter uses Unicode aware counting, which keeps multi code point emoji from being split across copies.
Is my text uploaded?::No. Repetition happens entirely in your browser. Your text is never stored or sent to a server, and the download is created locally as a text file. The file is created locally in your browser.
